title: Warranty Desk Embedded in Maintenance Software
one_liner: A white-label, success-fee warranty desk sold through mid-tier maintenance-tracking and MRO software vendors. The removal event, the PO and the repair invoice meet inside a system the operator already uses, and the software vendor earns a revenue share.
customer: The channel buyer is the partnerships or customer-success head at a mid-tier maintenance-tracking or MRO software vendor with 50-400 operator customers. The payer is the operator on that software: a regional airline, Part 135 or cargo-feeder fleet, or helicopter operator. The vendor pays nothing. It receives 30% of our fee and gets a renewal and differentiation story.
problem: Operators on these systems already hold structured removal, install, hours and cycles data, plus POs and receiving records. That is the data-access problem the parent idea could not solve. Still, warranty stays unclaimed, because the missing pieces are things software does not do. Someone has to read negotiated PDF terms, file on each shop's own template, and chase the shop for 60-90 days. Vendors cannot staff claims specialists. Operators' thin materials teams cannot absorb the work. The claim is decided at the removal moment, when a technician pulls a unit at 3 AM and nobody sees the terms. Only the maintenance software sees that event.
solution: The vendor gives a read-only export or API for removals, installs, POs and receiving. We load each shop's warranty terms from the operator's contracts and invoice PDFs. When a technician posts a removal against a serialized component, we return a lookup card in seconds, inside the vendor's UI or by email or Slack in the first version. The card shows who repaired the unit and when, the remaining window in days, hours or cycles, the evidence checklist, and a pre-drafted claim. Our claims specialists then file, chase and post the credit memo back into the system as a warranty record. A monthly sweep catches misses, late turn times, no-fault-found fees and open cores. Operators sign a contingency agreement. The vendor contract is non-exclusive and revenue-share only.
why_now: LLM extraction of warranty fine print and invoice PDFs means one specialist can now run claims for dozens of operators. Software vendors are also under pressure to prove value in the renewals of small and mid-size operators. Ramco advertises warranty-recovery savings, which shows the outcome is being marketed. Nobody sells the outcome as a service to the other vendors.
revenue_model: Operators pay 20% of cash and credits recovered, with a 12-month tail. The vendor gets 30% of our fee, about 6 points of recoveries, and owns the relationship. From year 2, vendors can bundle a Warranty Desk line item at $1-2k/month per operator, with us as wholesale fulfillment at about $600/month plus the success fee. Aggregated vendor-level claim data is a later product.
non_obvious_insight: Maintenance software has an adoption problem, not a feature problem. Warranty fields and modules sit empty because filling them takes human work: reading PDFs and chasing vendors. A managed service that makes the module produce cash is worth more to a vendor than building the feature. The vendor also supplies what our own sales cycle lacks: structured removal data, a warm introduction, and a trigger at the exact moment the claim is won or lost. Vendors will not build claim-chasing themselves. Terms are negotiated PDFs, and staffing claims desks is not a software margin.
first_30_days: Approach 8 mid-tier software vendors' partnership heads with a one-page offer: we make a slice of your customers' warranty tracking pay, with no cost to you and 30% of our fee. Ask each for 2-3 design-partner operators. Work as a concierge service, with no integration yet. The operator exports removals, POs and receiving from the software's standard CSV export, we match against invoice PDFs, and we deliver a ranked claim list with the vendor's customer-success manager on the call. Build the removal lookup as a simple web form or email responder. Sign a revenue-share MOU with the first vendor and aim for the first credit memo by day 30-45. Hire a retired materials coordinator for shop quirks. Success is 2 operators with live removal-time lookups by month 3.

It targets vendors that lack a warranty offering, and Ramco or its implementation partners remain possible channels. Trax, Veryon/Rusada, Pentagon 2000 and CAMP homepages showed no claims features, so they are the intended partners. The offer differs from an ERP module because it is done-for-you and paid only on results. It avoids the data-access problem by using the vendor's structured data. It also avoids cold sales to small operators, since the vendor's existing customer base and success team provide distribution.

title: Independent Post-Reform Valuation for Medical Lien Funders
one_liner: A neutral, coder-signed valuation agent that tells LOP factoring companies and the lenders behind them what their medical receivables are worth after tort reform.
customer: Regional medical-lien funders and LOP factoring companies in Florida, Texas and Georgia that buy receivables from ortho, pain, chiropractic and ASC providers, plus the warehouse lenders and private-credit funds financing them. Buyer is the funder's CFO or head of underwriting, with the lender's credit analyst as the forcing party. First target list is 30-40 funders.
problem: Funders buy receivables at a fraction of billed charges, priced on attorney reputation and past collections. Reform changes the collateral. In Florida, 768.0427 makes the LOP, coded billing, the factoring purchase price and referral relationship disclosable and admissible, and amounts actually paid become the reference point. Cases accruing after March 2023 are only now reaching settlement, so the first post-reform collection cohort is landing on funders' books. Their lenders want borrowing-base reporting and independent collateral valuation, and no neutral standard exists. Carrier vendors, plaintiff platforms and data utilities serve everyone but the person holding the risk.
solution: Phase 1, fixed-fee 'Book Audit' in 10 business days. The funder sends a de-identified export (purchase price, coded bill lines, provider NPI, attorney, venue, dates, outcomes on closed files). Output: cohort-level expected collection and time-to-cash curves under current state rules; the top-decile at-risk receivables; a signed independent valuation letter the funder can hand to its lender or investors; and a 'bid sheet' of maximum purchase price by CPT bundle, provider type, venue and attorney tier. Phase 2: per-receivable scoring at purchase and monthly re-marking through a portal or API. Phase 3: lender-appointed valuation agent, where the warehouse lender designates and co-signs the engagement and receives monthly portfolio monitoring, like a collateral field exam. The coder bench and methodology from the parent are reused, but the output is a valuation, not a courtroom opinion.
why_now: First post-reform (Florida 2023) case cohort is resolving in 2026, so books are repricing now and lenders are asking questions. Private credit has moved into esoteric legal and medical receivables, and lenders in that class expect third-party collateral valuation. Florida's mandatory disclosure of factoring purchase price means every funder now knows its own buy price is evidence against the receivable, which forces a rethink of pricing and structure. LLM bill extraction makes coding a 2,000-line portfolio in days instead of months, with coder sampling for sign-off.
revenue_model: Book Audit $15-40k per portfolio, repeated semiannually. Subscription $3-6k/month plus $12-25 per receivable scored. Lender-facing monitoring $2-4k/month per credit facility, mandated by covenant. Illustration: 30 funders at $60k/year is about $1.8M, with upside from expanding to hospital-lien, workers' comp lien and pre-settlement receivables, and eventually independent collateral valuation for rated securitizations of medical receivables, where third-party valuation is mandatory.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody has looked at LOP bills as collateral. The same benchmark that is a weapon in a deposition is a valuation input in a credit agreement, and the buyer has the best data. Funders hold the only ground-truth set of what LOP bills actually settle for, by code, provider, attorney and venue, which carriers, defense lawyers and every vendor lack. Serving funders buys that dataset and tightens every later model. The issuer-pays conflict that damaged rating agencies is solved by making the lender the appointing party and by fixed fees, like an ABL field examiner.
first_30_days: Pull UCC-1 filings (for example the Florida Secured Transaction Registry) that name medical receivables or accounts as collateral, to identify funders and the banks and credit funds financing them. Recruit two coders, one ex-ABL field examiner or credit analyst who has run a borrowing-base review, and one part-time attorney to build a rules matrix by state. Run a blind backtest pilot with 2-3 funders. They send 200-500 closed receivables with outcomes hidden, we predict the realized collection, they compare. Offer it free in exchange for permission to use the calibration. Convert the best pilot to an $18-25k Book Audit and use the result to approach that funder's lender.
lineage: mutation of I0428 ('Coder-Signed Reasonable-Value Reports for Injury Defense'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Enlyte (Mitchell/Genex) Demand Package Review and Bodily Injury Integrated Solutions, FAIR Health, EvenUp, Turquoise Health. White space: Caveat: the WebSearch budget hit its cap (200 of 200) before I could run the planned searches on startups, Crunchbase, Product Hunt and forums. This verdict rests on direct page fetches only. Treat 'gap' as provisional. Before building, someone should spend an hour on the searches I could not run: 'letter of protection medical bill review', 'reasonable value expert Florida LOP', and Crunchbase/YC for 'LOP' or 'defense medical bill'.

What I could confirm: no vendor I could reach sells a fixed-fee (about $300-700), fast-turnaround, coder-certified report with an optional declaration or testimony upsell aimed at LOP reasonable value. The nearest product is Enlyte's Demand Package Review. It is a carrier-side workflow product with nurse and analyst review at 3-4 to 10 days. It shows no coder signature, no LOP framing and no testimony. It also lacks the piece defense lawyers need most, which is a signed opinion that survives cross-examination. Data companies (FAIR Health, Turquoise) sell inputs, not signed opinions. EvenUp is plaintiff-side.

Specific white space: (1) small and mid-size defense firms and panel counsel who can't justify a $3-5k expert on a $30-100k claim. (2) Coder-signed output that holds up under cross-examination, tied to the LOP disclosure record. (3) States without a statutory benchmark, where reasonable value is contested.

Two weaknesses in the pitch. (a) Florida is partly commoditized by statute. Fla. Stat. 768.0427 (https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0768/Sections/0768.0427.html) already makes evidence of what was actually paid, or 120% of Medicare (170% of Medicaid where there is no Medicare rate), the benchmark for uninsured claimants. The fetched summary does not settle whether that applies to LOP treatment, so check the statute text. A large part of the Florida 'report' is therefore a Medicare-multiple calculation from free CMS files, which a claims shop or existing vendor could copy quickly. (b) The hospital price-transparency 'why now' is weaker than the idea claims. CMS says enforcement of the new rules starts April 1, 2026 (https://www.cms.gov/priorities/key-initiatives/hospital-price-transparency). But LOP care is mostly delivered by chiropractors, pain clinics, orthopedic groups and physician-owned ASCs, not hospitals. I inferred that from how LOP cases usually work and did not verify it. The defensible professional-fee benchmarks would come from Medicare multiples, payer transparency-in-coverage files or licensed data, not hospital files. | How this version avoids them: Enlyte and CLARA sell to carriers, and serving receivable buyers would create channel conflict with their own customers, so they rationally will not respond. EvenUp is plaintiff-side treatment and demand software and does not value receivables. FAIR Health and Turquoise sell charge and rate data, which we buy as inputs. JurisPro-style expert witnesses are litigation-only and have no portfolio product or lender-facing signature. The customer set is new to all of them. The parent's Florida commoditization problem disappears because the product prices collectability and duration, not a Medicare multiple, and our moat becomes proprietary realized-collection data plus the lender relationship.

title: Independent Auditor for AI-Paid Pet Claims
one_liner: A read-only shadow adjudicator plus a cross-carrier duplicate registry that independently re-checks every auto-paid pet claim against the policy's own clauses and produces the validation records state examiners now ask for.
customer: Head of claims and the compliance officer at US pet-insurance MGAs and small carriers paying roughly 100k-400k claims a year that already auto-adjudicate through a vendor platform or in-house LLM triage. The channel is the fronting carriers whose binders give them claims-audit rights over those MGAs. Narrowest wedge: MGAs that announced automation in the last 18 months and write in the 25+ states that have adopted the NAIC AI bulletin.
problem: Once claims are auto-paid, the insurer is accountable for the model's output but cannot see inside it, and the vendor selling the automation is marking its own homework. Two failures are invisible. One is silent overpayment: excluded lines paid (exam fees, cremation, prescription diets, supplements), wrong deductible, co-insurance, annual-limit or waiting-period math. The other is wrongful denial, which means complaints and market-conduct exposure. No single carrier can see the same PDF invoice filed with two insurers, or an altered invoice that looks fine in isolation. The parent's price-based edits add a third problem: reductions land on owners as balance bills, with no vet contract behind them, so mid-size insurers will not fund them.
solution: Read-only nightly export of invoice, policy form and adjudication decision, with no workflow replacement. (1) Normalize every invoice line to a canonical code (start from VeNom, so there is no taxonomy to defend). (2) Extract each policy form's exclusions, limits and waiting periods into clause-anchored rules once per form, human-verified. (3) Re-adjudicate independently and return agree or disagree per claim with a clause citation, sorted into three queues: likely overpaid, likely wrongly denied, and duplicate or tampered (PDF metadata, font and amount forensics). (4) Produce a monthly exam-ready validation pack with sample testing, drift and complaint linkage, which is what examiners request under the bulletin. (5) Cross-carrier registry: carriers contribute only hashed fingerprints (clinic, date, total, pet identity hash, line hashes) and get match alerts. Price benchmarks appear only as informational flags. They become a reason to reduce a payment only where the policy form has reasonable-and-customary language and the carrier opts in.
why_now: NAIC's AI model bulletin has been adopted by 25 states plus DC as of July 2026, and a 12-state examiner evaluation-tool pilot runs through September 2026. Under it, insurers stay accountable for vendor model outputs, and 'we cannot see the model internals' is not accepted. Pet premiums grew about 19% in 2025 on 6.98M insured US pets, and carriers are racing to automation (Five Sigma at Odie, Lassie at about 60% automated). LLMs make clause extraction from policy forms and PDF invoice reading cheap enough for a two-person team.
revenue_model: Annual platform fee of $45k-$120k by claim volume (about $0.15-$0.30 per claim scored), including monthly exam-ready packs. Registry-only tier of $12-25k for small carriers and TPAs. Optional 15% contingency on documented overpayments prevented on contract-clear lines. Sales math, assuming a $350 average paid claim: a 200k-claim MGA pays about $70M a year in claims, so an $80k fee breaks even at about 0.11% of claim dollars. Month-12 target: 6 MGAs at $80k plus 6 registry-tier customers at $15k, roughly $570k ARR. The registry then extends to all US carriers at a per-lookup fee, an ISO-ClaimSearch-style utility for pets.
non_obvious_insight: Regulation has turned automation from a cost saver into a liability, and the vendors selling automation are structurally unable to vouch for themselves, the way an accounting firm cannot audit its own consulting work. Independence is the product, and it is a budget line that exists (compliance, delegated-authority audits) rather than one that has to be invented. Duplicate and tamper detection is the only kind of edit that gets more valuable with every carrier that joins and never requires fighting a vet or a policyholder. State anti-fraud immunity statutes generally permit sharing suspected-fraud data with anti-fraud organizations, which makes a hashed registry lawful to seed on day one.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: map which MGAs and small carriers have publicly announced automation, and list the NAIC-bulletin states each writes in. Recruit an ex-claims QA manager as design partner. Days 7-21: build the clause extractor on 10 public policy forms and the invoice normalizer on about 500 sample invoices. Days 14-30: cold-approach 25 heads of claims and compliance with a free 'exam-readiness shadow audit' of 2,000 of their auto-approved claims from the last 90 days. The deliverable is a one-page count of overpaid lines, likely wrongful denials and duplicates. Convert the best results to a $25k, 90-day paid pilot. Success is 3 signed pilots by day 90 and a registry seeded by those pilots' fingerprints.
lineage: mutation of I1056 ('Unbundling Edits for Pet Insurance Claims'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: VetControl (Illingen, Germany), Five Sigma (Clive AI claims adjuster), Sirma (custom ML for PetsBest, now under Synchrony), FairVet. White space: Nobody I found sells a US, insurer-facing, explainable edit library (canonical line-item codes, bundling and duplicate rules, unit plausibility, reason codes) with cross-carrier benchmarks, to mid-size MGAs and TPAs.

- VetControl is the only true direct analog, and it is German, GOT-based, a services-plus-software hybrid, and shows no US customers.
- Five Sigma and Sirma classify line items for coverage, not for pricing or bundling.
- FairVet and Vet Receipt hold consumer-sourced benchmark data with no insurer-grade normalization.
- Trupanion and Lassie built in-house and are not customers.
- Verisk has standardized the policy side only.

The unserved gap is an invoice-derived, ZIP-level, procedure-level price index built from insurer claims, which no owner-upload app can match in volume. It would be joined to explainable pay/reduce/review decisions for mid-size carriers with no data science team.

Structural risk to flag. Human-health edits work because of provider contracts and CMS rules. Pet insurers have no contracts with vets and no 'global fee' concept, and they pay owners by reimbursement. Line-level reductions therefore land on policyholders as balance bills, which invites complaints and regulatory attention. I found no US insurer RFP or public spend for this. The demand evidence is indirect: cost inflation, plus vendors like VetControl selling a similar product in Germany. | How this version avoids them: Five Sigma, Sirma, and Lassie's in-house engine are the thing being audited, so they cannot sell independent validation. Five Sigma also does not describe unbundling or benchmarks, and Sirma is a bespoke services shop. Trupanion is in-house and never a customer, and we do not target it. VetControl is German, built on the GOT statutory fee schedule, names no US customers, and cannot read US policy clauses. FairVet and Vet Receipt are consumer bill-checkers with thin data and no insurer audit trail. Verisk's ISO pet program covers policy forms and rating only, so it is a possible acquirer or channel rather than a rival today. VeNom and SNOMED-VET are inputs, so the moat is the clause-to-line rule corpus, the pooled fingerprint registry and examiner-accepted evidence packs. Avoiding price-based reductions removes the balance-bill risk that the parent's research flagged.

title: Chute-Side Cow Counts for Ag Lenders
one_liner: Turn the vet's preg-check clipboard into a borrower-consented, third-party-verified herd inventory that banks can lend against.
customer: Community banks, Farm Credit associations and ag lenders with cattle loan books (they require it or pay per report, usually passed through to the borrower). Secondary payer is the cow-calf or heifer-development operator who wants bigger operating lines or bred-heifer financing on better terms.
problem: Cattle collateral has no VIN. Lenders verify with drive-by counts and borrower-supplied spreadsheets, and prosecutors in 2026 alleged a roughly $9.4M fraud that included a loan of $2.8M against 850 head. Farm loan delinquencies are rising while bred cows trade around $3,000+ per head, so a 500-cow borrower is $1.5M+ of collateral that nobody independent has counted.
solution: A 'Verified Herd Report' generated at the working day the vet is already doing. The vet or tech logs every head with an EID or visual tag scan (a $500 handheld reader plus a phone app), age class, pregnancy status and stage, and location. The vet e-signs and the borrower approves sharing with one tap. The lender gets a portal with timestamped, geotagged counts and year-over-year flags (head count down, pregnancy rate down, tags not matching last year). A second light pass happens at weaning. The vet earns a per-head fee for data they already write down and throw in the truck door pocket.
why_now: Federal EID ear tags became mandatory for many interstate cattle movements in Nov 2024, so per-head digital ID is now normal and cheap. Herd rebuilding at record cattle prices is being financed with debt, lenders entered 2026 carrying operating losses from 2023-2025 (rising delinquencies and restructures), and a fresh cattle-collateral fraud case is making ag loan committees ask for verification. Fall preg-check season is running right now (Sept-Nov).
revenue_model: $2-3 per head per verification, split roughly 50/50 with the vet practice, charged to the borrower or the lender as a loan condition. Add a portfolio dashboard for lenders at $500-2,000 per month once an institution has 100+ verified borrowers. Later, sell the verified inventory and pregnancy data to lenders as an underwriting input (advance rates on verified bred heifers).
non_obvious_insight: The vet is the only independent professional who physically handles every animal in the herd once or twice a year. They count, tag-check and pregnancy-check every cow, and that data dies on a clipboard. Vets refuse to police clients, but they will happily attest to what they handled when the borrower initiates the request, so the conflict-of-interest problem disappears. Honest borrowers are the real buyers: verified bred females can justify higher advance rates, and that cheap capital funds the fee many times over.
first_30_days: Preg-check season is live, so sign up 3 rural practices that each do several thousand head of fall preg-checks. Pitch 3-4 community-bank ag lenders (target the one who has been burned by a herd count before; work through state bankers' association ag committees). Run a pilot on about 10 willing borrowers with a form-based app and a PDF report, charging $2/head. Gather a before and after on what the lender learned that the drive-by inspection missed, then use that to sell the annual program.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global / Where Food Comes From (Beef Passport), Merck Animal Health (Allflex tags/readers, Vence). White space: Caveat first: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I ran zero searches. I did direct fetches of about 15 vendor and agency pages, plus GitHub repo searches. Nothing here rules out a direct competitor. The biggest gap is that I could not identify the third-party collateral-inspection firms that lenders already pay for cattle counts, or any startup selling vet-verified herd inventory to lenders. Do not treat 'gap' as 'open'.

What the direct fetches showed: none of the herd-software, EID, tracking or verification vendors I checked advertise a lender-facing 'independent count' product. The vendors were CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global/WFCF, Ceres Tag, Halter, HerdDogg and Gallagher. Merck/Vence returned 403, so I could not check it. Every one of them is a producer-side management or supply-chain tool. GitHub searches turned up no open-source lender-verification tool, only hobby herd apps.

The unserved wedge is a lender-mandated, third-party-attested herd inventory built as a covenant workflow. It would cover the vet-signed chute-side count, a portfolio dashboard, and year-over-year anomaly flags such as head count down, pregnancy rate down, or tags missing versus last year.

Structural weaknesses to be skeptical of:
- Adverse selection: 'borrower-initiated' verification means fraudulent borrowers never opt in. The product only works if lenders make it a loan condition.
- Coverage: a preg-check only counts animals brought to the chute that day, not cattle on other leases or sold or double-pledged since. It does not prove ownership or lien priority.
- Vet liability and willingness: vets may refuse to sign anything that reads as a collateral audit.
- Economics: $2-3/head split 50/50 leaves the vet about $1-1.50/head on top of a preg-check fee that is already several dollars.
- Entry by an existing vendor: IMI Global (WFCF) or Merck/Allflex could add this as a feature.

title: Placement Proof for Workforce Pell Providers
one_liner: A verified job-placement and completion ledger that makes short-term training programs (CDL, CNA, welding, HVAC, medical assistant, cosmetology) audit-ready for the governor and Secretary approvals that Workforce Pell requires.
customer: Small proprietary career schools, community college workforce and continuing-education units, and employer-training nonprofits running 8-15 week programs. The program owner or director pays. State workforce boards are a second buyer because they were given no new resources to verify placement.
problem: The Workforce Pell final rule (published May 19, 2026; effective July 20, 2026, with early implementation from July 1) covers programs of 150-599 clock hours and 8-15 weeks. A program must show 70% completion and 70% job placement, measured over the 12 months before it applies and annually after that. The governor must first certify the program as high-skill, high-wage or in-demand, then the Secretary approves. Providers must submit completer lists and the information needed to verify placement. Commenters flagged burden for small providers and noted states got no new resources to run the framework. Separately, the earnings-premium rule (effective July 1, 2027) strips Direct Loan access from programs that fail in two of three consecutive years. The Department estimated 93% of cosmetology programs would fail under the proposal.
solution: At completion the system automatically sends completers and employers text and email verification requests at 30, 90 and 180 days. It collects pay stubs, employer confirmations and consent for state wage-record matching, and reconciles them to the rule's placement definition. It produces the governor's application packet (completer list, placement evidence, tuition versus earnings benchmarks) and the annual recertification. It also scores each existing program's exposure to the earnings-premium test using public program-level earnings data so owners can decide what to keep, fix or convert into a short-term program.
why_now: The 12-month look-back means a provider that is not tracking verified placement now cannot apply in 2027. The earnings-premium test takes effect July 1, 2027 and is already being scored on 2021 completers' 2025 earnings. States are building governor-approval processes this fall, and Workforce Pell went live July 2026.
revenue_model: $4-12k per year per program subscription, or $150-300 per completer verified. $3-5k fixed fee for the governor application packet. Earnings-premium exposure report for $1.5-3k. Later, licensing to state workforce boards for verification.
non_obvious_insight: The binding constraint is not program design but evidence: 70% verified placement with a 12-month clock that starts before the application. Short-course providers such as CDL, CNA and barbering schools typically track completion, not verified employment, so most will discover the gap after the clock has started. The final rule requires providers to give the Governor 'necessary information to verify the job placement rate', and it aggregates small programs' completers up to four award years to reach a 30-student minimum, which favors providers with clean historical records. The Title IV survival angle (93% of cosmetology programs were projected to fail the earnings test under the proposal) gives the same customer a second, more urgent reason to buy. Sources: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/19/2026-10013/accountability-in-higher-education-and-access-through-demand-driven-workforce-pell-pell-grant and https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/07/01/2026-13286/accountability-in-higher-education-and-access-through-demand--driven-workforce-pell-student-tuition
first_30_days: Pick two states whose governors have opened a Workforce Pell approval process. Recruit five schools in different fields, including one at-risk cosmetology school, with a $1.5k pilot price. Backfill the last 12 months of completers by text and employer email to produce a baseline verified placement rate. Deliver a sample governor packet and an earnings-premium exposure score for each. Use the results to pitch the state workforce board on verification capacity.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ellucian (incl. former Anthology CampusNexus SIS, Occupation Insight), Populi, Gradelink, Lightcast. White space: Confidence is LOW. My WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200) before any searches ran. Only 9 direct page fetches went through, and they returned homepage-level content. I also tried a Google URL through WebFetch and then stopped, because that was an attempt to get around the search limit. I found no direct competitor, but I did not search for one, so this is not evidence that none exists. Homepage checks of Populi, Ellucian/Anthology, Gradelink and Lightcast showed no Workforce Pell or placement-verification features. Orbund's site was bot-blocked, and the Federal Register and ed.gov pages redirected or returned 403, so I could not check the rule text. Likely unserved wedge: a Workforce Pell-specific product that (1) backfills the 12-month look-back by contacting completers and employers, (2) reconciles evidence to the rule's placement definition, and (3) produces the governor application packet for small CDL, CNA, barbering and cosmetology schools. Not searched, so still unknown: startups or Product Hunt and YC entries; existing placement-verification services already sold to accredited career schools (ACCSC, NACCAS, COE reporting); consultancies selling this as a service; state-built portals; and SIS vendor Workforce Pell roadmaps. Structural risks visible without further research: (a) if the final rule lets states verify placement from UI wage records, a self-collected pay-stub product loses much of its value; (b) SIS vendors can bolt this on as a feature; (c) the number of approved programs, and so the buyer count, may be small at first.

title: Cure Desk: Cash-Worker Packets for Health Centers
one_liner: A Spanish-first text-message case tool for health-center enrollment staff that turns a Medicaid noncompliance notice (or a pre-emptive look-back audit) into a state-formatted evidence packet for cash-paid workers, built on batch attestations from the crew leaders, landlords and households who pay them, billed per accepted packet.
customer: Enrollment and patient-navigation managers (certified application counselors, community health worker leads) at FQHCs and community health centers whose panels are heavy with day laborers, house cleaners, landscapers, roofers, temp-agency and informal restaurant workers, and street vendors. Narrow wedge: one Nebraska health center with a large Spanish-speaking panel (plus one refugee language), then a second state that verifies early. The end user is the patient in a 15-minute session with a CHW. The patient installs nothing and pays nothing.
problem: The parent idea was a self-serve wallet sold to MCOs. Judges flagged slow MCO procurement, weak enrollee adoption, and the IFR limiting plans to a support role. The competitor check found SteadyIQ and Emmy giving states free or bundled bank, payroll and gig linking, and Pointcare and Findhelp already holding the FQHC and MCO relationships. What none of them can serve is the worker with no digital trail. The IFR counts self-employment, gig work and in-kind work and lets people combine activities, so someone who cleans three homes for cash and helps on a landscaping crew is legally compliant but has no payroll record, no bank deposits to link, and a 30-day cure clock the day a notice arrives. Timing nuance: an HFMA summary of the IFR says self-attestation is allowed through 2027 (and once per beneficiary in 2028), so the documentation wall arrives in waves. Early-verifying states and audit-driven renewals come first, the general wall later. The first-year job is therefore both cure packets and building an audit-proof evidence file in advance.
solution: Six pieces. (1) Notice intake: the CHW photographs the notice, or the patient forwards it on WhatsApp or SMS. OCR extracts state, case ID, look-back months and deadline, and a 30-day countdown lands in the CHW queue. (2) State evidence rule pack: a maintained library of what each state and program accepts (in-kind work, combined activities, third-party statements, receipts), calibrated by logging every accept and reject reason. (3) Attester rail: the patient names who paid them, and that person gets a text in their own language ('Did Ana Ruiz work for you in August? About how many hours or how much did you pay? Tap to confirm'), creating a timestamped third-party statement in the state's format. Crew leaders, labor contractors, property managers, day-labor centers and church job boards get a batch screen that confirms 5 to 30 workers in one pass, with a reusable profile. (4) Packet: a PDF or portal-ready bundle with the hours or $580 computation, attachments and the patient's e-signature. The CHW submits as authorized representative, and the tool never decides compliance. (5) Outcome capture: accepted or rejected plus the caseworker's reason feeds the rule pack and billing. (6) Routing: patients who do have a digital trail are handed to the state's own Emmy or SteadyIQ consent flow, and exemption flags such as medical frailty are asked as a triage question only.
why_now: The June 3, 2026 IFR sets a Jan 1, 2027 start and a 30-day cure window, and six-month renewals for expansion adults begin around the same time (verify exact start), so notices and renewal checks multiply from Q1 2027. Nebraska is already live and is expected to move from self-attestation to verification. WhatsApp Business API, cheap OCR and LLM translation make a bilingual, photo-based intake cost cents per case, where a bilingual caseworker hour costs roughly $30. That is what makes a 15-minute assisted cure economical for a health center. In 2019 this would have needed a call center.
revenue_model: Per-case fee to the health center: $40 when a packet is opened plus $110 when the state accepts it (max $150, inside the parent's $50-150 range), with a $750 per month per-site minimum. Flat per-case fees rather than percent of Medicaid revenue keep it clean under inducement and billing-agent concerns (healthcare counsel to confirm). Channel revenue: white-label the packet builder as an API or module inside Pointcare, Findhelp or other health-center platforms at a 20-30% revenue share. Illustrative year-1 math (assumptions): 20 health centers x 40 packets a month x $120 average x 12 = about $1.15M. Later: a state-accepted-evidence data license to navigators and legal aid.
non_obvious_insight: Informal work is clustered behind intermediaries. One crew leader, property manager or household employer can attest for many workers at once, so each new attester makes the next patient's evidence nearly free, and the same attester serves patients at other health centers. The hardest segment for bank-linking vendors, where every cash worker is a costly manual exception, becomes the one segment with a network effect. The scarce asset is not the ledger but knowing what each state's caseworkers actually accept, which can only be learned by filing packets and logging outcomes. That data compounds with every case and cannot be bought or scraped.
first_30_days: Week 1: sign one Nebraska FQHC (or health center with a large Spanish-speaking panel) for a free concierge pilot, and call the state Medicaid policy office and two caseworker offices to ask which third-party statements are accepted as evidence. Weeks 2-3: build the flow from a Twilio or WhatsApp number, a Google Form, and a PDF template, with a bilingual attester text. Have the CHW enroll 25 real cash-paid patients and collect at least 40 attestations. Week 4: file the packets, or run the pre-audit in a state that is not yet verifying, and record acceptance rate and CHW minutes per case. Target: 60%+ acceptance and under 30 minutes a case versus 2+ hours today. Then take the numbers to a second health center and to Pointcare and Findhelp as a module partner.
lineage: mutation of I0573 ('Medicaid Hours Wallet for Gig Workers'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CMS Emmy (Eligibility Made Easy) app and Emmy API, SteadyIQ (Income Passport / Verification Hub), Digital Public Works, Maximus, Optum, Acentra, Deloitte, Gainwell, Conduent, Curam/Merative (state-side community engagement modules). White space: Nobody I found sells an enrollee-side monthly ledger to MCOs or FQHCs that ingests bank, gig and pay-stub data, computes $580 or 80 hours against a state's look-back rules, and produces a state-specific 30-day cure packet. Nothing turned up in searches, CMS vendor pledges or CBPP/KFF/Georgetown landscape coverage. Vendors sit on either side of that gap. State-side vendors (SteadyIQ, Emmy, Maximus, Optum, Deloitte) sell to state agencies. Provider and plan-side vendors (Pointcare, Findhelp, mPulse) sell eligibility monitoring and outreach without gig-income packet building. The clearest unserved segment is workers with no digital trail: cash, informal and 1099-below-threshold workers such as day labor, cleaning and landscaping. Consent-based verification (CBV) via payroll, bank or gig platforms cannot reach them. The 30-day cure step, meaning a compiled packet after a noncompliance notice, is also not addressed by any product I found. The wedge is narrow and could close quickly. States with CBV (SteadyIQ, Emmy) let the enrollee connect accounts directly, which makes a separate packet redundant there. MCOs may be poor buyers because the IFR bars plans from determining compliance and gives them only a supporting role. Pointcare and Findhelp already own the FQHC and MCO relationships and could add a module. Research limits: my web search budget ran out after four searches, so I relied on page fetches. I could not load the CBPP vendor landscape, the Health Affairs piece or the Federal Register text (all blocked), and I could not confirm what Propel for Plans does or any vendor's funding. | How this version avoids them: SteadyIQ and CMS Emmy: they win wherever a bank, payroll or gig account can be linked, so Cure Desk does not compete there and routes those patients to their consent flows. It serves only the cash and informal residue, where their cost per case is highest. Free state-side tools and the vendor pledges (Maximus, Optum, Acentra, Deloitte, Gainwell, Conduent, Curam) are sold to states and track hours. Cure Desk is a staff workflow sold to health centers. Pointcare and Findhelp: they do lapse detection and dashboards without informal-income packet building, so they are channel partners, not rivals. Propel and mPulse do notices and outreach, and CareRoute is informational. None builds attester-backed evidence. Digital Public Works is a nonprofit focused on mobile income verification. It is adjacent, and could become a partner or a free-riding substitute in some states (risk to monitor). Buyer choice removes the parent's MCO procurement and IFR-role problems.

title: Replication Bench: Poll-Triaged Experiments With Signed Records
one_liner: A poll-first replication service: anonymous postdoc consensus tells biotech investors and AI-bio builders which claim to test, and a pool of laid-off bench scientists runs the decisive experiment and returns a signed, machine-readable execution record.
customer: Seed and Series A biotech VCs, corporate venture arms and pharma BD teams evaluating spinouts (poll memos and replications). AI-first biotechs and AI-for-science startups with agent swarms and no wet lab (ticketed experiments). Later, licensees of the replication registry.
problem: Investors can buy candid consensus but can't cheaply convert it into a test. Agent-driven startups can buy experiments, but cannot tell which literature claims their designs are built on. A bench network alone has speculative, nascent demand from agents. A poll shop alone has no way to run the decisive experiment.
solution: Bench Pulse: within 5 business days, 8-15 vetted, paid, anonymous subfield postdocs and senior techs give a structured memo on the named claim (consensus, red flags, fragile reagents, what to test first). Where the poll narrows the question, the same team runs 'Key-Figure Replication' at rented bench space with pre-registered success criteria. Each job returns a signed record separating protocol, human edits and physical execution (deviations, photos, instrument logs, raw data). AI-agent customers order the same protocols through an API and can request 'claim-verified' runs before building on a paper.
why_now: There is a large pool of laid-off molecular biologists and postdocs available at near-market rates, seed funds are scrutinizing academic-spinout claims harder, and AI-for-science startups are producing agent-designed experiments faster than anyone can run them.
revenue_model: $4-6k per poll memo, $15-40k per key-experiment replication, $30-60k per year fund retainers for pipeline-wide bench pulse, $1.5-8k per agent experiment at roughly 35-45% gross margin, and later licenses of the labeled replication registry to AI-bio firms.
non_obvious_insight: Poll consensus is the cheap triage that decides where a $15-40k replication is most informative, so the bench network needs less capacity to make more money per experiment. Each replication then scores the poll: 'polls predicted X of Y outcomes' becomes proof that lets the company sell poll-only memos at scale. Every job adds to a labeled dataset of what replicated, what didn't and why, in a machine-readable format, which is precisely what AI-for-science companies lack and can't obtain from papers.
first_30_days: Pick one subfield where you personally know about 20 contacts (for example CAR-T, organoids or targeted protein degradation) and draft the NDA and anonymity protocol (about $3k in legal). Recruit 10 laid-off molecular biologists, sublet 2-3 surplus benches, and define a fixed-price ticket type for replication. Offer 3 seed funds a free poll on an asset they are already reviewing, convert one to a paid $5k poll, and upsell a replication. Pitch 10 AI protein-design startups on the same bench.
lineage: hybrid of I0400 + I0868 (Bench-Truth Diligence for Biotech Investors + Human Bench Network for AI Agents). Why stronger: Each parent has a missing half: bench-truth diligence lacks capacity to run the decisive experiment, and the human bench network lacks a buyer with an urgent budget and a filtered question. Together, a $5k poll funds triage, a $15-40k replication uses the bench, and the labeled replication registry becomes a moat that neither Hoeford-style polls nor cloud labs can build.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Hoeford Research, Alacrita, Fios Genomics, GLG. White space: Caveat on coverage: the WebSearch quota was exhausted (200 of 200) before this task started. I substituted direct WebFetch of competitor pages, Google News RSS, and some Brave and Bing queries. Brave rate-limited me (429) and Bing returned junk. Hoeford and Fios pages were blocked or truncated. So 'nothing found' is weaker than a full sweep, and the founder should confirm with Crunchbase and LinkedIn plus 10 calls to seed VCs.

What I found. Both halves of the idea have adjacent players, but I found no one selling the specific product as described.

Poll half. Expert networks (GLG, Guidepoint, Third Bridge) and scientific-diligence boutiques (Alacrita, Fios) all sell expert input to investors. They interview senior experts and KOLs, sell bespoke projects, and market to finance clients. I found no fixed-price, 5-day, named-claim consensus poll of 8-15 anonymous junior bench scientists. That is a real wedge, and it fits the founder's critique that the incumbents rely on conflicted seniors.

Replication half. 'Wet diligence' at CROs or independent labs is an accepted practice (LifeSciVC says it should be 'gating before investing'). Hoeford appears to sell it. Science Exchange has the marketplace and the history (Reproducibility Initiative, RP:CB). The bundle, where the poll narrows the question and then a pre-registered, blinded replication follows, looks unserved. Owning a bench pool of laid-off scientists is the least defensible and most operationally risky part.

Segment. AI-bio founders building on published wet-lab claims are the least served, but Adaptyv Bio (raised $40M, 3-week assays from $149 per protein) is already serving protein-design validation.

Structural threats.
- GLG or Guidepoint can copy the poll cheaply once it is proven, since they already sell surveys.
- Anonymity is leaky in subfields of 20-50 people.
- Postdocs risk their careers and may breach university confidentiality or employment terms.
- A negative poll about a named PI's paper carries defamation and tortious-interference exposure.
- A replication that fails in a new lab does not prove the claim is false, which is the ambiguity buyers hate. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Adaptyv Bio (Adaptyv Biosystems), Ginkgo Bioworks (Cloud Lab and Datapoints), Emerald Cloud Lab, Science Exchange and Scientist.com (CRO marketplaces). White space: Things I did not find. I could not run WebSearch (the session budget of 200 was used up), so this comes from Google News RSS queries and direct page fetches. I did not check Crunchbase, YC's directory, Product Hunt or GitHub in depth; a GitHub repository search returned nothing.

1. No funded company sells human-executed, ad hoc, arbitrary-protocol wet-lab work through an agent-native ticket API with a fixed price and a signed record separating AI proposal, human edit and physical execution. The nearest pieces are split across companies. Adaptyv has the agent API but runs standardized automated assays. CRO marketplaces have custom human work but run on quotes and SOWs. Transfyr has the execution-record capture but no labor. Emerald and Ginkgo have flexible automation but were not found to offer human-run ad hoc work to agents.
2. The long tail beyond fixed assays is the actual gap. That means multi-step, protocol-specific molecular biology that a robot cannot be programmed for in time: novel enzyme or nuclease activity validation, cloning plus cell-free expression plus a custom activity readout, and unusual cell-culture assays. Anthropic's post confirms this is where a frontier lab keeps human scientists.
3. Nobody I found sells biosafety-screened human execution of AI-proposed protocols as a service, even though oversight of AI-directed experiments is in the news (Lab Manager, 'Biosafety Oversight for AI-Directed Lab Experiments', Sept 28, 2026; Frontiers paper on automated-lab security tiers).

The window is narrow and closing.
- Adaptyv has $40M, agent-native positioning, a stated plan to add 'more complex biological workflows', and Chai and Boltz as customers. It can move toward the ad hoc tail with automation.
- Scientist.com and Science Exchange could add an agent API or MCP layer around their existing providers with modest effort.
- Transfyr could bundle records with any CRO.
- Anthropic and other frontier labs are insourcing bench capacity.

Risks to the idea's own claims:
- BioSpace headlines show layoffs are easing: August 2026 biopharma layoffs were about 500, down 90% year over year, and the Q2 job report says postings are rising. Skilled hands are still available, but the 'layoff wave' supply story is weakening (via https://news.google.com/rss/search?q=biotech+layoffs+2026+BioSpace+job+cuts+tracker).
- Sublet-bench operations carry insurance, contamination, quality-control and IP-chain-of-custody risk that a software-style API hides.
- The 35-45% gross margin at $1.5-8k per experiment is unproven against commodity CROs and against Adaptyv's automation, which starts at $149 per protein for screening-level binding.

title: Pooled Calendar Reporters for Limited-Scope Family Lawyers
one_liner: One physically present reporter sits an entire family-court calendar and sells the record by the matter, about $110 per 15-minute hearing, so each lawyer pays roughly 75% less than a half-day pro tem while the reporter earns more than a normal pro tem day.
customer: Wedge: limited-scope (unbundled) and solo family-law attorneys who appear on DVRO, custody and support calendars in ONE high-volume California courthouse, plus the non-indigent 'missing middle' litigants they represent, who fail the fee-waiver test but cannot spend $450 on a record. Not indigent litigants (the FVAP ruling moves them to a court-paid record) and not the court.
problem: About 7 in 10 civil, family and probate hearings in California have no verbatim record, and appeals of custody and restraining-order rulings fail without one. Courts tell litigants to 'arrange your own' reporter, but a private pro tem costs $450-500 for a half day, and no one pays that for a 12-minute item. The parent's fix (remote reporters dialing in) is barred by Gov. Code 69959 and by the 69959.5 pilot limits, so it cannot launch as written. The parent also has no proof that anyone will pay $95, and the ruling shrinks the legal-aid segment.
solution: Drop remote reporting and prediction. A reporter is physically in the department for the whole morning or afternoon calendar, which is the lawful 'bring your own reporter' route. Attorneys book a matter slot the day before at $110 for up to 15 minutes, plus a per-page certified transcript (about $8/page) only if they order one. Booking is all-or-nothing, like a crowdfund: the reporter goes only if at least 6-8 matters are booked by 5pm the day before, otherwise everyone is refunded. That kills the dead-time problem without any duration model. Each party gets only its own matter's transcript, and other matters on the reporter's notes are never released. Cross-department hopping and duration prediction come later, once the manual logs give real data. Unit economics (assumptions to test): 2 sessions/day x 8 matters x $110 = $1,760 gross. The reporter keeps about 60% ($1,056) versus $900-1,000 for two half-day pro tem bookings, and the company keeps about $700 per reporter-day before ops.
why_now: FVAP v. Superior Court (Aug 10, 2026) put the 70% no-record gap in every family lawyer's inbox. It also makes courts serve only indigent litigants, which leaves a large paying middle. Courts are already telling family litigants in writing to arrange their own reporter. The reporter shortage (about 5,500 short by 2030) means freelancers can choose better-paying days, so a higher-yield day is a real recruiting pitch.
revenue_model: $110 per matter slot for up to 15 minutes, $8/page for certified transcripts, and prepaid 5-packs ($500) for cash up front. The reporter keeps about 60% of slot fees, the platform keeps about 40% (about 35% gross margin after the payment and ops costs of a services business). Year-2 add-ons: a subscription for attorneys who book 8+ hearings a month, and referral-funded 'record scholarships' from DV appellate nonprofits.
non_obvious_insight: Once the first attorney in a department triggers the reporter's presence, every other matter that day costs roughly nothing extra, so the price can fall 75% while the reporter's day pay rises. Limited-scope attorneys are the right buyer because they bill flat per hearing and can pass the record fee through as an itemized line, while a full-service litigator does not think of the record as a per-hearing line item. The tipping-point booking rule replaces the prediction model the parent needed.
first_30_days: Week 1: one-week legal check with a court-reporter licensing attorney and the clerks of the 2 target departments (private pro tem in the room, multiple parties sharing one reporter, closed-hearing rules, and any court-reporting-firm registration). Weeks 1-2: pick the single biggest family courthouse in one county, recruit 3 physically local pro tem reporters, and pre-sell 5-packs to 15 limited-scope attorneys from the family-law bar and unbundled-services listservs. Weeks 3-4: run the first 10 calendars with a Google Sheet, Stripe links and a group text, using the booking threshold, and log booked-matter density and actual call order per department. Offer FVAP and one DV appellate nonprofit free slots for cases they flag as appeal-bound.
lineage: mutation of I0248 ('Fifteen-Minute Court Reporting for Family Law Hearings'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Steno (Steno Agency Inc.), DirectDep, StenoScout, Incumbent agencies (Veritext, Esquire, Combs Reporting, Coalition Court Reporters). White space: Nobody offers flat-fee coverage of 15-minute California family-law hearings. That is because the core mechanic, private reporters dialing in from anywhere, is currently barred. Gov. Code 69959 says 'Remote court reporting shall not be used by courts to make the record of any court proceedings' and defines it as a stenographer not present in the courtroom (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959/). The only exception, Gov. Code 69959.5, allows remote reporting only by 'full-time official reporters ... employed by the participating superior court', physically in a court facility, in 13 pilot counties, capped at 10-20% of reporters (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959-5/). San Diego's court page states 'the court is prohibited by law from allowing remote court reporting for any court proceeding' (https://sdcourt.ca.gov/sdcourt/generalinformation/resourcelists/courtreporterinformation). The idea's claim that AB 3013 'opened remote reporting' to a private platform is wrong. Unserved and still legal: (1) physical-presence short-hearing coverage, where one pro tem covers several departments in the same courthouse using calendar-based duration prediction, and no vendor markets a per-hearing SKU; (2) a scheduling and utilization layer sold to courts to fill pro tem and official reporter slots, aimed at hiring and retention (the ruling names 'pro tem reporters paid by the court' as a compliance route, and court reporter counsel is calling on courts to lift hiring freezes); (3) fast certified transcripts of court electronic recordings for attorneys who need appellate-grade records. The white space is real but is a legal-regime bet on remote reporting being opened to private reporters, plus a narrow physical-hopping wedge. It is not a software-only wedge. Court reporter unions opposed AB 3013 and are a political headwind. | How this version avoids them: Steno, DirectDep, StenoScout and the agencies (Veritext, Esquire and others) sell a whole appearance to one buyer, mostly depositions, so every buyer pays the full minimum, and their half-day minimum is structural. We sell the matter, split one appearance across many paying parties, and stay lawful without remote reporting. The AB 3013 pilot covers only court-employed reporters in a court facility, capped at 10-20% of reporters in 13 counties. We serve paying litigants in any county and do not compete for the court-employed slots. eScribers and Verbit transcribe recordings, which fits the court's indigent fallback but not an attorney who wants a stenographic record, live and immediate. The moat, if the wedge works, is proprietary calendar density and call-order data per department, and reporter loyalty from the higher day yield, which points to a cornered-resource advantage in one courthouse before any scale.

title: Lead Line Photos Taken During Meter Swaps
one_liner: Add a 90-second, three-photo service-entry protocol with on-device AI to the water-meter change-out crews a utility already sends into basements, and sell it to the utility as a $10-14 per line change order.
customer: Mid-size water utilities (30k-150k connections) in the Northeast and Great Lakes that have inside-set meters, an active or planned meter or AMI replacement program, and more than 30% 'unknown' service lines in their inventory. Two budget owners: the AMI/meter program manager (capital project change order) and the lead program manager (compliance budget). The meter-installation contractor is the channel and co-beneficiary. Wedge account: a utility whose meter contractor has not yet mobilized, so the protocol goes into the statement of work.
problem: Unknown lines stay unknown because access is the hard part. Mailer self-ID reaches 10-25% of owners, and absentee landlords and LLCs almost never answer. The parent idea's paid-photo network has three weak points. First, opportunistic supply (home sales, water-heater swaps) is thin per utility. Second, the state may treat photos from third parties as self-ID-grade evidence, because the rule appears to require identification by 'water system personnel' (verify by state). Third, inspectors may not accept the liability of calling a pipe lead. Meanwhile utilities are paying crews to enter the very same basements and stand within about 3 feet of the service entry for every inside meter swap. Those crews record a meter serial and nothing about the pipe.
solution: An app or SDK for the meter crew. Photo 1 shows the pipe where it enters the wall, upstream of the meter valve. Photo 2 is a scratch and magnet close-up, using a $0.50 test card in the installer's kit. Photo 3 shows the meter serial and pipe together, which ties the evidence to the account. On-device checks reject blurry or ambiguous shots while the tech is still standing there ('retake, pipe not visible'). A vision model classifies the pipe as copper, galvanized, lead, plastic or unresolved. Low-confidence cases go to human QA and, for unresolved or mixed-material lines, to a probe or pothole queue. The tech never labels a pipe, which removes the liability concern. Output is a reconciled inventory feed in the state portal format, pushed into the utility's Esri layer, plus a dashboard showing unknowns falling by ZIP. Techs get a small per-verified-set bonus so they don't skip the step.
why_now: Meter fleets from the 2000s-2010s AMR wave are hitting battery and end-of-life, and cellular sunsets have pushed utilities into funded AMI change-outs (verify local schedules). These are the few funded programs that put a utility contractor inside every home in a specific neighborhood. State inventory updates and the 10-year replacement clock (federal details are still being litigated and revisited, and several states have their own statutes) mean unknowns carry real cost and a deadline. On-device vision models now catch bad photos at capture time, so the crew does not have to be an expert. SRF and infrastructure-law money rewards utilities that shrink unknowns before applying for replacement funds.
revenue_model: Per-line fee of $10-14 billed as a change order to the meter deployment contract, or as a per-utility deployment license of $60-150k. Change orders in that size range often clear without a council vote. Rough unit economics per line: installer bonus $2-3, kit $0.50, AI and QA $2-3, hosting and support about $1, leaving about $5-6 gross margin (roughly 45%). A 40k-inside-meter deployment is about $480k of revenue. Add-ons: inventory reconciliation SaaS, and later a resell of the same feed to meter contractors as a bundled 'verification-ready' option in their bids.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not a photographer, it is legal access. Every water tariff already makes meter access a condition of service, and utilities enforce it with repeat visits and shutoff notices, so meter crews reach exactly the absentee-landlord and LLC homes that no self-ID portal can reach, at a marginal trip cost of zero. The crew is also water system personnel or contractor, so the evidence sits in the strongest evidentiary class the state rule seems to allow. And the pipe at an inside-set meter is usually the same pipe the lead rule cares about, a few feet from where the crew is already working. A separate paid-photo marketplace has to build access, supply and trust. This borrows all three from the utility's own procurement.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: list every utility in two states that has inside meters, an announced meter or AMI program, and a public inventory over 30% unknown. Call the AMI program manager and the lead program manager at 15 of them. Also call three meter-installation contractors and ask whether they'd add a photo step for a per-set bonus. Days 10-20: get one state drinking-water program to say in writing whether a visual verification by utility-contracted personnel can reclassify an unknown. Prototype the capture app with real-time retake prompts and a scratch and magnet card. Days 20-30: run a 300-home pilot inside one utility's existing swap route, priced at cost as a change order. Validate the classifier against 100 lines the utility already knows (historical records, prior replacements) and against 20-30 potholes. Publish the accuracy and per-line cost, and propose a full-route contract at $12.
lineage: mutation of I0463 ('Pay Home Inspectors to Find Lead Pipes'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: BlueConduit, VODA.ai (Lead Finder / Lead Zero / Lead Management Dashboard), Trinnex leadCAST (used by Durham, NC), Esri ArcGIS Lead Service Line Inventory solution. White space: Nobody I found runs the specific thing proposed: a paid supply-side network of trade professionals (inspectors, plumbers, water-heater installers) who photograph the service entry under a fixed protocol, with vision-AI classification, tamper-evident geo-verification, human QA, and export to state inventory formats, sold to utilities per verified line. Players fall into four groups. (1) Predictive modelers (BlueConduit, VODA.ai) reduce digs statistically but still need ground-truth field samples, and Texas does not accept predictive modeling for official inventories. (2) Customer self-ID portals (Trinnex leadCAST, Esri Survey123, Cognito Forms) collect photos and reach only the 10-25% of owners who respond, and absentee landlords and LLCs almost never do. (3) Hardware probes (Electro Scan, Echologics) need a utility crew at each line. (4) Door-to-door inspection programs (RCAP, engineering firms) are staffed centrally and slowly. The unserved wedge is professional-grade evidence for the non-responding, owner-absent lines at about $30-60 per line, collected by people already inside the building. Two sub-gaps stand out: states that reject modeling but accept documented visual verification, and small or mid-size utilities with no field crews. Caveats: (a) my WebSearch budget ran out after 4 searches, so Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and GitHub sweeps were not done and a stealth or very early startup in this niche could exist; (b) the search snippet says physical identification methods 'must be conducted or overseen by water system personnel' (state-dependent), so third-party photos may only count as self-ID-grade evidence unless the utility or state accepts contractor verification; (c) the idea's own note that regulatory details are from memory still applies; (d) per-utility supply is limited to home sales and water-heater swaps, so density per utility could be slow; (e) inspectors may resist liability for calling a pipe lead (my recollection, unverified); (f) Trinnex or Esri could add a 'contractor submission' role cheaply. | How this version avoids them: BlueConduit and VODA.ai predict statistically and still need ground truth. This produces deterministic evidence for 100% of the homes the crew visits and can be sold to them as calibration data. Trinnex leadCAST, Esri Survey123 and the Chesterfield and Massachusetts DEP forms all depend on owners responding, and they reach 10-25%. Tariff-backed meter access is a lever they do not have. RCAP door-to-door inspections, Electro Scan probes and Echologics/Mueller acoustic tools all need a dedicated visit or crew per line. This rides a trip that is already paid for. Stantec and other engineering firms bill field crews hourly, so a $12 add-on cannibalizes their revenue and they are more likely to resell it than build it. Trinnex or Esri adding a contractor role would not reach into the meter-deployment workflow, which the installers and utilities own. The parent's inspector network is dropped as the primary channel, which removes the cold-start, the liability objection and the third-party evidence problem.

title: Independent Big-Meter Audits With Refund Guarantee
one_liner: A brand-neutral audit of a utility's 100-400 largest meters: AMI history is turned into a ranked, field-tested list of under-registering accounts. It is sold as a fixed-price small purchase, refunded if verified annual recovery is under 2x the fee.
customer: Finance director or utility director at a combined water+sewer municipal utility with 10-40k connections. AMI (or monthly-read AMR) is fully deployed, there are 100-400 meters of 3 inch and larger, and there is no in-house crew to bench- or field-test large meters. A rate hearing or rate study is due within 9 months. Wedge accounts: hospitals, hotels, food and beverage plants, universities and laundries. These run all night on low flows, which is exactly where old compound and turbine meters under-read.
problem: The parent's ghost-parcel half is weak (permits trigger taps, ADUs are usually billed on a shared meter) and contingency contracts are restricted or slow in some states. Back-billing is legally capped and politically toxic. The real leak is quieter. The utility's most valuable meters are 15-30 years old and lose low-flow registration. The meter is also the instrument that would have to report its own failure. Every under-read gallon is lost twice, because sewer charges on commercial accounts are billed off the water read. Councils are approving 5-10% rate steps while nobody has tested the top-revenue meters. Meter vendors and distributors do test large meters, but their business is selling the replacement.
solution: Step 1: get one CSV of 24 months of reads or interval data for the top 100-400 accounts, plus the meter inventory (size, make, install year). Step 2: compute a 'low-flow fingerprint' per account: (a) share of hours with zero registered flow versus use-code and NAICS peers that show base load; (b) a hole in the flow histogram just below the compound-meter crossover or start-up flow; (c) step-downs after meter or endpoint changes; (d) zero-read or estimated-read streaks. Step 3: rank by expected annual dollars, water plus sewer. Step 4: an independent crew field-tests the top 12-15 (three flow rates, AWWA M6-style, in-situ rig) and issues test certificates. Step 5: deliver a council-ready 2-page brief ('this recovers $X a year and offsets Y points of the next rate step'), a brand-neutral replacement spec, and prospective-only correction as the default. Recovery comes from swapping the meter, not from back-billing. The measured under-registration also replaces the default assumption in the utility's AWWA/M36 water audit and raises its Data Validity Score.
why_now: Utilities that finished AMI in 2018-2022 now hold 4+ years of hourly data that no one has analyzed for revenue. PFAS, lead-line and pipe capex are forcing rate hikes into affordability fights, so 'prove we've fixed our own leaks first' is a strong council story. State water-audit mandates (for example Texas for systems with 3,300+ connections) create an annual moment when apparent losses are examined. Cheap data engineering means a two-person team can build the fingerprint model. Incumbent meter makers have no credible way to tell a customer that their installed base under-registers.
revenue_model: Fixed fee of about $24k (scan plus 12 independent tests), priced under typical small-purchase or informal-bid limits (to verify per state), refunded in full if verified annualized recoverable revenue is under 2x the fee. Add-ons: $1.5k per meter for post-swap verification; an annual 'Big Meter Monitor' at $8-15k a year per utility; licensing the screen to rate consultants and AMI vendors. An opt-in success share applies only in states where it is lawful, for ghost-parcel or sewer-only leads. Assumed unit economics: about $10k COGS per audit (about 30 analyst hours, 12 subcontracted tests at roughly $600-800). About 55-60% gross margin and about 30 audits a year for two people is roughly $700k, before monitor ARR.
non_obvious_insight: A refund guarantee on a fixed fee gets the benefits of contingency (zero risk, easy yes) without the parts that block contingency: percentage-of-recovery bans, RFP thresholds and 'paid to find money' optics. The defensible asset is not the model. It is a private labeled dataset of field-test accuracy by meter make, model, size and age matched to its AMI fingerprint. Only a party with no meters to sell can collect it, and each audit adds about 12 ground-truth labels. Recovery is mostly prospective, so the back-billing fight in the parent version never happens.
first_30_days: Pull the 'principal water customers' table from five target utilities' public annual financial reports and the state rate-study calendar. Pick 15 utilities with 10-40k connections and a hearing in the next 9 months. Offer a free 5-business-day screen of the top 100 accounts from one CSV. Line up a test-rig subcontractor and an AWWA-experienced water-loss advisor. Test the top 3 leads at the first free screen for free, using the findings as the proof case. Pre-sell one paid audit with the guarantee to a utility whose hearing is scheduled. Confirm the small-purchase limit in the first two states. Also test the unverified claim that large meters are 40-60% of revenue by checking the annual financial reports.
lineage: mutation of I0388 ('Contingency Hunters for Unbilled Water Revenue'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Itron (Temetra Analysis / Non-Revenue Water portfolio), Badger Meter (BEACON, OneNetwork), Master Meter (Harmony Encore MDM), Metron-Farnier (WaterScope). White space: Important caveat: my WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before any of my searches ran. This verdict rests on about 20 direct page fetches and GitHub repo searches, not on broad web, Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt sweeps. Treat 'no direct competitor found' as unconfirmed, and do a manual pass on Crunchbase, YC and RFP portals before committing. What I did verify: (1) I found no vendor selling a contingency-fee service that joins assessor roll, footprints, imagery and the billing system to produce named unbilled addresses for water utilities. (2) The metering and analytics incumbents (Itron, Badger, Master Meter, Metron) sell software tied to their own hardware, with no evidence of a ranked, dollar-denominated, legal-ready recovery list or contingency pricing.
