Genuinely unserved: an independent, outcome-priced screen of large-account meter accuracy that ranks specific accounts by expected dollars using consumption history, and that does not depend on one meter vendor's hardware. Ghost-parcel discovery is the weaker half. A structure with no account is rare where permits trigger taps, and an ADU on a shared meter is usually already billed on consumption. Back-billing is politically and legally messy, and some jurisdictions restrict contingency contracts. The larger risk is structural (yield, procurement law, optics), not competitive. | How this version avoids them: Itron, Badger, Master Meter and Metron-Farnier sell analytics tied to their own meters and networks, with no independent account-level audit and no credible way to tell a customer that their own meters under-read. We are meter-brand-neutral and sell no hardware. Contract test firms and distributors test to sell replacements, so we are the conflict-free verifier. The AWWA free audit works at system level with an assumed meter-error percentage, so we feed measured values into it instead of competing with it. Rate consultants (Raftelis, FCS, Hazen) do fee-based apparent-loss reviews at system level with sampling, not ranked account-level dollars with test certificates. EagleView and imagery vendors solve parcels, not meters. We drop ghost parcels as the headline and avoid the contingency-contract and back-billing exposures the parent's research flagged.

title: Grid-Readiness Model Audit for Data Center Lenders
one_liner: An independent checker for private-credit funds, banks and delay-in-start-up insurers that audits a borrower's large-load models and ride-through evidence and gives an energization-risk opinion, the same way financial-model auditors already serve project-finance lenders.
customer: Data center and GPU-cloud finance teams at credit funds, banks and ABS arrangers, plus the lender's independent engineers, technical advisors and project-finance law firms that act as the channel. Delay-in-start-up (DSU) insurers and MGAs are the second payer. The borrower's fee is paid at lender direction, which is the market norm for lender advisors.
problem: Lenders finance billions of dollars of campuses and GPU fleets. Interest accrues and hardware depreciates while the site waits for energization. Their diligence covers construction cost, schedule, MEP and offtake, but grid dynamic behavior is a black box authored by an interested party: the borrower's own consultant says interconnection is on track. After the 2024 Northern Virginia load-loss event and ERCOT's new rules, lenders have no independent way to judge whether the load model will pass, whether ride-through settings will trip the site, or how far energization could slip. Developer-side consultants such as Electranix and Danovo are conflicted, and the lender's independent engineer typically lacks EMT skills.
solution:
Sell a check, not a build.
1) A pre-close Grid-Readiness Opinion of $30-75k per site. It is an independent review of the borrower's PSS/E and EMT models, study reports, interconnection-agreement conditions and UPS, PSU and firmware settings against the ISO's rules and generic reference models. It ends with a red/amber/green rating and a P50/P90 energization-slip range.
2) A conditions-precedent and covenant kit for law firms: draw conditions such as ISO-accepted model, passed ride-through test and firmware freeze.
3) Re-attestation of $10-20k whenever GPU generation or UPS firmware changes, triggered by covenant.
4) A portfolio dashboard for lenders by ISO and site, and an anonymized risk dataset for DSU underwriters.
Analysts run rule-based checklists and scripted checks through the PSS/E Python API, so each review takes about 40-80 hours. Our own modeling is never required.
why_now: Neocloud and data center debt (delayed-draw term loans, GPU-backed facilities, ABS) grew explosively in 2025-26, and energization delay has become a visible schedule risk in publicly reported neocloud results. Regulatory rules that make models and ride-through a gating item are now in force in Texas, with PJM and NERC large-load work following. Lenders and insurers are looking for a diligence item to price, and nobody offers it yet.
revenue_model: Borrower-paid, lender-directed fees of $30-75k per site per financing and $10-20k per refresh re-attestation. DSU insurers pay $10-25k per underwriting review, or a data license, and later take a share of premium through an MGA program. Rough bottom-up: 200 qualifying US financings a year (assumption to verify) at $50k is about $10M, and 400 sites refreshed at $15k is about $6M, so this is a $15-25M niche. It is a thin, high-margin analyst business that later becomes a rating or registry.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer of a grid model is whoever bears the cost of delay, not the grid. Project finance already has an independent-checker culture, with financial-model audits and independent engineers, because lenders will not trust numbers authored by the borrower. A dynamic load model is the same kind of black-box spreadsheet driving a billion-dollar decision. The parent's three structural threats become tailwinds here. Free EPRI or NERC generic models become the benchmark we audit against. OEM secrecy is irrelevant because we test the borrower's model against acceptance criteria and measured behavior and need no OEM IP. In-house hyperscaler tools do not matter because hyperscalers are not project-financed on this basis. Independence is the moat, which the developer-side consultants cannot claim.
first_30_days: Run 15 interviews: 5 data center finance leads at credit funds and banks, 5 lender independent engineers or technical advisors, 3 DSU underwriters or brokers, and 2 project-finance law firms. Offer a $25k pilot Grid-Readiness Opinion on one live financing. Sign one independent-engineer firm as a white-label channel, since it can bill our add-on and lacks EMT capability. Recruit one ex-ISO planner and one project-finance analyst. Publish a 20-question Grid-Readiness Diligence Checklist for lenders and a redacted sample opinion built from public queue and rule data, and pass it through law firms as collateral.
lineage: mutation of I0996 ('Grid-Code Models for AI Data Centers'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Typhoon HIL (Data Centers solution), OPAL-RT (HYPERSIM, power-HIL), EPRI DCFlex, Emerald AI (Emerald Conductor). White space: Across this session's research I found no direct competitor selling packaged, hardware-validated large-load dynamic models (PSS/E plus EMT) with ride-through study reports and certification letters for GPU-cluster, PSU and UPS stacks. Nobody was seen selling OEM-level type-test certification for power shelves and UPS platforms. Adjacent players cover only pieces: HIL tools (Typhoon HIL, OPAL-RT), generic EMT consultancies, EPRI's flexibility consortium, workload-flex software (Emerald AI), and simulation software vendors with no data center library shown.

Three structural threats need answers:
1. Regulators and EPRI or NERC may publish free generic composite or EMT models, which commoditizes the model library.
2. OEMs (UPS, PSU, NVIDIA) own the confidential control details and may ship their own models.
3. Per-project EMT consulting already exists and is not verified either way for large loads.

The defensible white space is independent, hardware-validated, ISO-acceptable model packages and compliance evidence for the 25-500 MW neocloud and colo developers who lack in-house power simulators. It would be reused across sites through OEM platform type tests, not sold as bespoke studies.

Research limits: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before this task began, so competitor discovery relied on direct page fetches and GitHub search. Startup databases (Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt), news, and NERC or EPRI publication pages were not checked. Several NERC, EPRI and PJM URLs returned 404 or empty content. Treat the 'no direct competitor' finding as moderate-confidence. Verify manually against NERC LLTF outputs, EPRI data center model reports, and WECC or ERCOT model requirements before committing. | How this version avoids them: No listed competitor sells to lenders or insurers. Typhoon HIL and OPAL-RT sell tools to engineers. EPRI DCFlex serves operators and utilities. Emerald AI sells flexibility to operators. Pearl Street speeds studies on the developer side. Electranix and Danovo are hired by developers and are structurally conflicted, so they become the supply of models we audit rather than competitors. Financial-model auditors do not have power-systems skills. Independent-engineer incumbents lack EMT capability, so they become the channel. Hyperscaler in-house tools are irrelevant because the customer is the debt-financed neocloud or colo borrower. Risk: a large independent engineer could hire EMT staff, so we must lock in the lender relationships and the covenant templates early.

title: Outside-In Product Security Ratings for Insurers and Buyers
one_liner: Invert the desk: instead of helping one maker meet the 24-hour clock, independently measure from the outside whether thousands of connected-product makers can, and how exposed their shipped firmware is, and sell the scores and accumulation data to insurers, fleet buyers and lenders.
customer: First buyers: cyber and product-liability insurers and MGAs writing hardware and IoT makers, who need product-level exposure and accumulation data. Second: B2B fleet and infrastructure buyers (EV-charging operators, micromobility fleets, smart-building integrators, telcos buying CPE) that run supplier due diligence. Third: lenders and PE firms doing diligence on hardware brands. Manufacturers do not buy scores. They pay only for evidence review and remediation (a funnel to the desk).
problem: Every maker will soon say 'we comply' with the CRA, but the declarations are self-assessed and unverified until a market surveillance authority acts, which is slow and under-resourced. Insurers have no product-level model of accumulation, even though one exploited component hits every device on that stack. That is a catastrophe-modelling problem with no model. Procurement teams rely on questionnaires. The 24-hour clock is uniquely measurable: it is a dated, binary behaviour, unlike vague 'security posture', but nobody measures it from outside.
solution: A rating built outside-in from three layers. (a) Clock-readiness signals: security.txt, a published CVD policy, a working vulnerability contact, advisory history, stated support period, update cadence, and time-to-acknowledge on a clearly labelled contact-verification probe. (b) Firmware exposure: public firmware and OTA images, plus purchased units for top SKUs, unpacked and matched against exploited-vulnerability feeds to give a component list, exposure count and stack cluster. (c) Portfolio accumulation: for an insurer's book of insureds or a fleet buyer's supplier list, how many share a stack with a newly exploited component (the correlation number). Makers get a right of reply and can submit evidence, but cannot pay to change a score. Method: month 0-3 process-signal ratings for about 500 brands across e-mobility, smart home, routers, chargers, cameras and wearables; month 3-6 firmware exposure on the top 200 SKUs and the first accumulation reports. A separate analyst team runs the desk as the remediation upsell, behind a conflict-of-interest firewall.
why_now: The reporting duty went live on 11 Sep 2026, so 'time to report' just became a legal, checkable behaviour. Insurers are pricing CRA-driven product liability for the first time. Outside-in ratings are a proven category for company networks, and firmware unpacking is now cheap through open-source tooling and LLM-assisted triage. No dominant product-level rating exists.
revenue_model: Data licences of EUR 25-80k/yr per insurer or MGA; EUR 6-15k/yr per fleet operator or integrator per category; EUR 3-8k per diligence report for lenders and PE; EUR 2-5k per maker for evidence review; desk upsell as a funnel. Long term the rating is written into insurance pricing and procurement clauses ('supplier must hold a score of B or better'), giving standard-setter economics with a data moat.
non_obvious_insight: Insurers care about accumulation more than any single score, and the desk's pooled stack graph is exactly an accumulation model, so the same data serves the desk and the rating. Real filings and drills, with consent and anonymised, give a calibration set showing which outside-in signals predict actual time-to-report, and that validation is what makes a rating credible. Every desk client both funds and calibrates the rating. Flaw of the inversion: legal risk (defamation, unauthorised access), which is why probes are labelled, analysis uses lawfully obtained units and public images, scores are aggregated and methodology is public.
first_30_days: Weeks 1-2: build a crawler over 500 brands in 6 categories to score security.txt, CVD page, contact deliverability, advisory history and support-period statements. Week 2: send a benign, clearly labelled contact-verification probe and record response times. Week 3: publish a free report, 'State of vulnerability-reporting readiness among 500 connected-product brands' (for example, what share have no working vulnerability contact weeks after the duty began), to earn press and insurer attention. Weeks 3-4: hold 20 discovery calls with cyber/product-liability underwriters, MGAs and fleet operators, and offer paid pilots of EUR 8-15k to score their insureds or suppliers. Aim for one signed pilot by day 45 and confirm that no insurer-grade product rating already exists before scaling.
lineage: mutation of I0374 ('Outsourced 24-Hour Vulnerability Reporting Desk (CRA)'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: TridentSec (PSIRT-as-a-Service), Finite State (managed CRA service), Cybellum (managed PSIRT / incident response service), Patchstack (managed CRA Article 14 reporting for open source). White space: The genuinely unserved piece is a contractually guaranteed 24/7 desk that files as the client's named Assigned Representative on the SRP, priced for 20-500 person device makers.
- Nobody found sells this in that form. TridentSec sells operations with no stated 24/7 and no published price. Finite State and H-X draft the notice but leave filing to the customer. Cybellum's service targets enterprises. CVD Portal, CRA Evidence and other tools stop at timers and packages, and their final filing is a human step by the customer. Patchstack files as AR but only for open source, and free.
- The intake step is also unserved: nobody takes weekend and night hits on 'is this KEV/EUVD entry in our firmware' and makes the call inside the 24h window.

What is not white space:
- The SBOM-to-CVE matching layer is commoditised. CVD Portal's Reporting tier is EUR 99/mo, and CRACI, Zealience, Regulus and ONEKEY sell the same thing.
- Boutiques and large consultancies can add 'PSIRT retainer' as a line item in weeks.
- The idea's claim that there is 'almost no visible tooling' is wrong. The service layer is thin, but the tooling layer is crowded.

Structural problems to plan around:
- The CRA fine exemption for micro and small enterprises on the 24h deadline (Art 64(10), https://cra-facts.com/penalties) removes the sharpest fear driver for the smallest customers. The 72h and 14-day deadlines still carry fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover.
- The SRP requires each AR to use a personal EU Login with MFA (https://www.enisa.europa.eu/topics/product-security/single-reporting-platform-srp/frequently-asked-questions), so named analysts must sit in the loop.
- Liability stays with the manufacturer, and the desk needs professional indemnity cover.
- The 24h clock starts when the manufacturer becomes aware, so a desk that spots an exploit may start the client's clock.
- An actively exploited vulnerability in one specific product's components is a low-frequency event. The retainer therefore risks being seen as insurance that customers only buy under audit pressure. | How this version avoids them: The parent's competitors (Finite State, Cybellum, ONEKEY, Cybeats, CVD Portal, CRA Evidence, CRACI) all work inside-out for the manufacturer's own firmware or workflow and are paid by the maker. This business is outside-in and paid by the party that bears the risk, so none of them competes for that buyer, and several become data suppliers. From general knowledge, not verified in this session: company-level ratings such as BitSight and SecurityScorecard score networks, not shipped products; certification schemes (ioXt, ETSI EN 303 645-based tests, UL programmes) are pass/fail, point-in-time and manufacturer-paid; consumer-testing NGOs publish periodic tests. Large MSSPs and certification bodies are conflicted because manufacturers pay them. The moat is the calibrated stack graph, the methodology and eventual adoption in insurance and procurement contracts.

title: Delay-Suit Rails for Stuck Immigration Cases
one_liner: White-label filing infrastructure that lets solo immigration lawyers file mandamus/APA delay lawsuits in 48 hours, turning the government's habit of mooting suits into a flat-fee product.
customer: Solo and small immigration firms (1-10 attorneys) who pay a per-filing platform fee; end clients (naturalization, green card and employment petition applicants) pay the firm a flat $2.5-5k. Secondary buyer: employers with stuck petitions.
problem: Cases are stuck well past posted processing times: interviewed N-400s never scheduled for oath, I-485s and I-140s idling, and holds or pauses applied to nationals of dozens of countries since late 2025. Clients wait 12-30 months. Lawyers know a federal delay suit often shakes a case loose, but most solos have never filed one. Drafting the complaint, civil cover sheet, summons, service on the U.S. Attorney's civil process clerk, the Attorney General and the agency, and district-specific local rules is a 6-10 hour learning curve, and no one wants to be the first to file.
solution: A web tool with three parts. (1) An eligibility screen: enter the receipt date, form type and field office, and it compares them to posted times and to real observed outcomes, then scores the delay claim. (2) A complaint and exhibit generator with a per-district rules library, a service-of-process checklist and deadline calendar (the 60-day government answer window), and a template for the joint status report or stipulated dismissal that follows adjudication. (3) A docket-outcome database that logs, by district, judge and case type, how long from filing to adjudication. The attorney of record signs every filing. The platform is software, not a law firm.
why_now: Through late 2025 and 2026 USCIS added enhanced vetting, holds and pauses on benefit requests tied to nationality, expanded re-review of approved cases, and slower naturalization and green card scheduling. The volume of genuinely stuck cases is at a decade high. Federal courts are also less deferential to agencies since the Loper Bright decision, and adjudicating a stuck case is cheaper for the government than defending it. Solos are overloaded and short of billable-hour alternatives, so a ready-made product for a high-ticket service is easy to sell.
revenue_model: $350-600 per filing charged to the law firm (flat, not a percentage, to avoid fee-splitting rules), or $299/month for up to 3 filings. Later: a paid intelligence tier of docket-outcome analytics by district, and a litigation-funding partnership for clients who can't front the fee.
non_obvious_insight: The lawsuit is rarely litigated to judgment. The U.S. Attorney's Office usually tells USCIS to adjudicate within 30-90 days so the suit can be dismissed as moot, so the client's real purchase is a forced deadline. Clients almost never hear about this because form-prep firms earn on the application, not on pressure. Posted processing times are also misleading (they reflect only completed cases at a percentile), so whoever accumulates real time-to-decision data by field office and district owns the moat.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 immigration attorneys in high-volume districts (N.D. Cal., S.D. Tex., D.N.J., E.D.N.Y., S.D. Fla.) and offer free templates for the first filing. Build the intake screen and three complaint templates first (delayed N-400 after interview, delayed I-485, delayed I-130/I-140 or a nationality hold). Concierge-run 10 filings by hand, charging the firms $400 each. Log every outcome date, since that dataset is the product. Post outcome stats to immigration-lawyer Facebook groups and AILA chapter listservs to pull in the next 30 firms.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Bertollini / Mandamus.com (immigration mandamus boutique), Docketwise (immigration case-management software), Alma (tryalma.com, immigration law firm plus tech), Boundless (consumer immigration services). White space: Important caveat first. The WebSearch budget was already spent (200 of 200) before I started, so I ran no web searches at all. I used direct fetches of guessed or known URLs, CourtListener's API and GitHub search. This means 'no direct software competitor found' is weaker evidence than normal. One attempt to load a Google results page returned nothing and was not used. Before committing, someone should run 6-8 real searches (for example 'mandamus AI immigration', 'delay lawsuit software immigration attorneys', Crunchbase, YC, and the AILA and AIC toolkits).

What I found: no software or platform that sells attorney-signed, white-label mandamus filing plus a per-district rules library plus outcome analytics to solo immigration lawyers. The only direct-service players are boutique law firms selling the suit to end clients. Mandamus.com does this at $5,000 plus $500 and gives away templates, and the practice-management incumbent Docketwise has no such feature. The open data (CourtListener) and free guides make the raw ingredients cheap for anyone.

The genuinely unserved wedge is narrow. It is a pre-filing 'will this get mooted or dismissed here' triage, based on real district-by-form-type outcome data, plus a ready-to-file pack for routine delays in the districts where the government usually adjudicates rather than litigates (per Mandamus.com's own data: EDNY, D. Conn., DNJ and EDMI at 83-85% voluntary dismissal after agency action).

Parts of the pitch look weak against what I found:
(1) Nationality-hold suits look poor. Per Mandamus.com's summary of 13 D.D.C. delay decisions from June to August 2026, the government won all 13. Judge Leon in the consolidated Ivanov case found the categorical pause unexplained but dismissed the delay and mandamus counts under TRAC and limited relief to named plaintiffs. A 'nationality hold' template is a liability, not a hook.
(2) S.D. Tex., one of the five launch districts, is hostile. Cheejati v. Blinken (5th Cir. 2024) bars I-485 delay claims on jurisdictional grounds, and DOJ there files motions to dismiss rather than negotiate.
(3) Buckhannon: when USCIS simply adjudicates, the plaintiff is not a prevailing party and can't recover EAJA fees (typically $4,000-$12,000 only if a consent order is obtained). The flat fee holds up, but the 'forced deadline' product should be structured around consent orders.
(4) The '6-10 hour learning curve' is being eroded by free content and general AI drafting.
(5) The data moat is thin. CourtListener docket data is free, and the boutique firms already publish their own district stats.

title: Data Act Broker for Equipment Owners
one_liner: File and operationalize EU Data Act data-access demands so independent service shops can finally read the diagnostics that elevator, heat-pump, forklift and tractor makers lock away.
customer: Independent maintenance and service companies in the EU (starting with elevator/escalator maintainers, then commercial heat-pump installers, forklift and ag-machinery shops). They pay per monitored asset per month. Equipment-owning businesses (building managers, hospitals, logistics sites) are the secondary payer, because they hold the legal right.
problem: Original manufacturers use exclusive access to machine diagnostics and fault logs to keep 60-80% of the lucrative service market. Independents work blind, so they lose contracts to OEMs. The EU Data Act (applicable since 12 Sep 2025) gives the user of a connected product, including a business, the right to get the data the product generates. The user can also have it handed to any third party of their choice. In practice almost nobody exercises the right. The paperwork is unfamiliar, OEMs stall, and the data arrives in a different format from every vendor.
solution: An agency-plus-plumbing service. (1) Sign a user-authorization letter with the equipment owner. (2) Auto-generate and file the Article 4/5 access and third-party-sharing requests to each OEM and track statutory response deadlines. (3) Ingest whatever comes back, whether an API, a file dump or a portal export. (4) Normalize it into one cross-vendor schema per asset class. (5) Give the independent shop a fleet-health dashboard and fault-prediction alerts. Add a public compliance scorecard showing which OEMs comply, and escalate the ones that do not to national enforcement authorities.
why_now: The Data Act became applicable on 12 Sep 2025. On 12 Sep 2026, 16 days ago, its design obligation started applying to newly placed connected products, so data must be accessible by default. The right-to-repair movement is at peak momentum. OEM stonewalling now generates complaints that regulators must act on. No one has industrialized user-side requests yet, so the first mover sets the standard schema and templates.
revenue_model: Setup fee of about 50-150 EUR per asset for the request and integration work, plus 4-12 EUR per asset per month for the normalized feed and health analytics. Add-ons: predictive-maintenance alerts and a white-label owner portal. Later: sell anonymized cross-fleet reliability benchmarks to insurers and asset owners.
non_obvious_insight: A legal right is worthless until someone industrializes exercising it. The Data Act gives the data-access key to the owner, not the repairer, so the winning business acts as the owner's agent and sells the result to the repairer. The moat is accumulated request templates, OEM-by-OEM response knowledge, and one normalized schema. Every OEM refusal also becomes evidence for regulators, which turns compliance friction into marketing.
first_30_days: Pick one vertical and one country pair, for example independent elevator maintainers in Germany and the Netherlands, and reach them through trade associations. Retain a Data Act lawyer for a fixed fee to finalize request templates. Recruit 5 independent shops, get user-authorization letters covering about 50 units, and file the requests. Log every OEM response and format. Charge a pilot fee of about 1-2k EUR per shop for delivered data plus a first fleet report. Publish an OEM response-time tracker to build inbound demand. Expect uneven enforcement, so keep the pilot to OEMs that respond and use the ones that stonewall as regulator evidence.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: High Mobility, agrirouter (cross-manufacturer agricultural data exchange), Jaltest / Cojali (Jaltest Diagnostics and Jaltest Telematics), OEM-owned platforms (KONE API portal; Otis ONE, Schindler Ahead and TK Elevator MAX are from my background knowledge and not verified this session).
