Crunchbase, YC, TechCrunch and Product Hunt were not checked, and Crunchbase returned 403. The verdict rests on direct page fetches and GitHub searches only, so treat 'gap' as moderate-to-low confidence. Re-run with the budget raised before committing money.

Within those limits, I found no product that files Data Act Article 4/5 requests on an equipment owner's behalf, tracks OEM responses, and normalises the returns across OEMs for independent service shops. Every adjacent player is either an OEM platform, cars-only (High Mobility), farmer-facing (agrirouter), on-site diagnostics (Jaltest), or OEM-side compliance code (GitHub kits). Genuinely unserved: (1) the owner-mandate plus request workflow, (2) an OEM-by-OEM response and refusal log, (3) a cross-OEM schema for lifts, heat pumps and forklifts, (4) the independent maintainer as the paying customer.

Structural weaknesses to fix in the idea:
- No fixed response deadline. As I recall Articles 4-5, data holders must respond 'without undue delay'. I could not fetch EUR-Lex to confirm (its WAF blocked me), but the idea's 'track statutory response deadlines' looks wrong.
- Article 5(1) lets 'a party acting on behalf of a user' request data. The independent shop can therefore file the request itself with a signed mandate. The broker's moat is then normalisation and OEM knowledge, not legal standing. Model letters and the Commission FAQ (v1.4, 22 Jan 2026) will commoditise the templates.
- Article 9 lets OEMs charge data recipients reasonable compensation, with a cost cap for SMEs, so OEMs may bill the shops you serve.
- Only 'readily available data' is covered. OEMs will argue that diagnostics are derived data, or invoke trade-secret and security refusals under Article 4(6)-(8). Safety-critical elevators are the likeliest place for a security argument.
- Article 4(1) design-by-default applies only to newly placed products, and old lifts often have no OEM connectivity.
- Tractors and other ag machinery may already have sector-specific repair-information access rules under type-approval law (Reg. 167/2013, from memory, unverified), which weakens ag as a beachhead.

title: Nonrenewal Desk for Colorado Independent Agencies
one_liner: An agent-side triage-and-evidence service that starts when a Front Range nonrenewal or score-disclosure notice lands, and charges most of its fee only when the policy is saved.
customer: Owner-principals of independent insurance agencies in Boulder, Jefferson, Larimer, El Paso and Douglas counties. Each has 150+ wildland-urban-interface homeowner policies, is appointed with 6 or more carriers so it can re-market, and has received several nonrenewals or surcharge notices since January 2026. Colorado only. California is dropped until AB 75 is confirmed enacted.
problem: When a nonrenewal or score disclosure arrives, the agent has about 10 days to get an acknowledgement and about 30 days to a decision (HB25-1182). The agent has no verified evidence, and the free homeowner kits (FireRisk.ai, Defensible Space Score) only produce letters. A corrected score may not move the premium, because insurers can meet the law with a manual mitigation discount and do not have to accept third-party imagery. The agent loses the commission and the bundled auto and umbrella policies, roughly $600 a year or more per WUI household.
solution: The agent forwards the notice PDF and gets three things within 48 hours. (1) A Lot Ledger: dated 15-50 cm imagery and public lidar canopy and clearance measurements set against each feature the insurer disclosed. Each feature is marked contradicted, confirmed or unknowable. (2) A Credit Map: for each carrier the agency is appointed with, which filed mitigation credits or underwriting-exception paths the evidence supports, so the pack asks for the premium or retention outcome and not just a score change. (3) A carrier-formatted pack timed to the 10 and 30 day clocks, plus a re-marketing shortlist when the appeal is weak. The desk declines to file when the evidence does not contradict the score. That keeps the concession ledger clean and makes carriers trust the packs. After trust is built, the same imagery layer is run across the agency's whole WUI book to flag likely errors before renewal.
why_now: HB25-1182 has been in force since July 1, 2026, so disclosures, appeals and the 10/30-day clocks are now real for every Colorado WUI policy. Independent agents are the ones absorbing the nonrenewals. Public regional aerial flights, USGS-style lidar and cheap commercial archives mean the first appeals need no imagery licence. I did not verify that insurer appeal desks are unprepared, so the plan does not rely on it; the trigger is the notice itself.
revenue_model: $249 per month per agency, including 5 triage runs and a book scan of up to 300 WUI policies. Extra packs are $149 each. A flat $300 success fee applies per policy retained or re-marketed within 90 days of a pack. There is no percentage of premium, to avoid producer-compensation and rebating problems. At 20 agencies, that is about $60k in subscriptions plus roughly $90k in success fees, around $150k ARR, with gross margin above 70% once imagery is bought per filed case only.
non_obvious_insight: The product is a decision about what will actually change the outcome: fix the input, harden the house, or re-market it. It is not a rebuttal letter. Honest triage is the moat, because a desk that refuses weak cases gets a higher concession rate, and a concession ledger keyed by carrier, vendor, input error and evidence type becomes something carriers cannot get elsewhere. Carrier-side vendors like Zesty, Nearmap and Cotality cannot sell against their own customers' scores. That is counter-positioning.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 Front Range agencies through a Colorado independent-agent association or by direct outreach to principals. Run concierge delivery by hand with an analyst using public imagery, lidar and QGIS, with no licensing. Give the first 5 files per agency free and charge $99 from file 6. Aim for 40 real notices and 20 filed appeals with outcomes tracked. Send agencies a private weekly concession scoreboard as the sales asset.
lineage: mutation of I1148 ('Parcel-Level Rebuttals to Wildfire Insurance Scores'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: FireRisk.ai (RiskIntel AI), DefensibleHome Wildfire Insurance Survival Kit, Defensible Space Score (AACI Group / Five Bays Insurance Agency), Road Home Exteriors 'insurance-grade verification packets'. White space: Nobody found sells imagery-based, parcel-level, insurer-format rebuttal evidence, and nobody sells an agent or HOA 'scan the whole book for likely score errors' workflow. What exists is (a) free or $99 homeowner letter and template kits with no imagery (FireRisk.ai, DefensibleHome, Defensible Space Score), (b) slow on-site certifications (IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home, Wildfire Partners), (c) contractor evidence packets sold with hardening jobs (Road Home Exteriors), and (d) carrier-side imagery scoring (Zesty, Nearmap/Betterview, Cape, Cotality, Verisk) with at most a compliance 'framework' for appeals. Specific unserved wedge: multi-date 15-50 cm imagery that shows a lot's actual condition (irrigated, gravel-scaped, recently cleared) against a 30 m coarse-layer score, formatted for Colorado's 10-day acknowledgement and 30-day decision clock, delivered to independent agents who carry many clients. Genuine caveats that shrink the gap: (1) The premise for California looks broken. AB 75's status page shows it 'held under submission' in Appropriations on 08/29/2025 and no source found shows it enacted (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB75). The CA DOI's own report reportedly says there is no formal appeal process. So the 'statutory appeal right' in CA is unverified and Colorado is the only confirmed regime. (2) Colorado HB25-1182 (signed 28 May 2025, effective 1 July 2026, https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb25-1182) requires disclosure of the score, range and a plain-language explanation of features. It does not clearly require raw model inputs (fuel class, vegetation density), and it does not require insurers to accept third-party imagery. The 'pull the disclosed model inputs' step may be thin, and DOI enforcement is only that the Commissioner may request a copy of a denied appeal. (3) Insurers can satisfy the law with a manual mitigation discount, so a score correction may not change the premium. (4) Free and $99 substitutes cap willingness to pay for $149-299 per file. (5) Zesty, Nearmap and Cotality hold the same imagery and the carrier relationships, so the durable moat is the concession database, not the imagery. | How this version avoids them: FireRisk.ai and DefensibleHome sell homeowner letters and templates with no imagery and no verification. This sells verified evidence and a decision to agents, who buy per book and not per household. The Defensible Space Score is free and self-reported, and the desk is what an agent uses when self-reports fail. IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home and Wildfire Partners are slow on-site certifications, and they become a channel later. Road Home Exteriors bundles packets with hardening jobs and does not scan books or work the clocks. Zesty, Nearmap, Cape, Cotality and Verisk are carrier-side and conflicted, and the desk does not compete with their scoring. The risk that one of them bolts on a policyholder module is met by locking in agency distribution and the concession ledger early, and by considering a data partnership with one of them.

title: ITAR-Safe Identity for New-Space Startups
one_liner: An identity layer that proves a new hire is real, where they actually are and whether they may legally see spacecraft technical data, then feeds that attribute straight into SSO and PLM access controls.
customer: Series A-C launch, satellite and defense-space startups (50-500 staff) and their sub-tier machine shops and avionics suppliers, reached through space-focused investors, accelerators and SpaceWERX/SBIR cohorts. Buyers are the head of security or compliance and the CFO.
problem: Space startups are hiring at breakneck speed, with remote engineers and contractors, into a Golden Dome-driven market (cost estimate raised to $185B) and nine-figure funding rounds. Giving a foreign person access to technical data is an ITAR export violation, and North Korean IT-worker schemes have reached 70 to 100+ US companies. Standard IDV proves someone is real, not whether they are a US person, and HR and ATS tools do not carry export-control eligibility as an access attribute. Fake suppliers and counterfeit parts add a second exposure.
solution: (1) Verify person and US-person status using document and injection-resistant liveness (partner with an existing IDV vendor rather than building it). (2) Check presence over time (VPN and laptop-farm signals). (3) Write 'US person, permitted data categories' into Okta or Entra groups and PLM and repo permissions through SCIM. (4) Supplier onboarding with KYB, sanctions and counterfeit-part red flags. (5) An auditor-ready evidence pack for CMMC Level 2 assessments and export-compliance reviews.
why_now: The DoD's CMMC rollout reaches its second phase on 10 Nov 2026, when third-party Level 2 certification starts appearing in contracts, and small suppliers are scrambling. North Korean worker prosecutions in Apr and May 2026 put hiring fraud on boards' agendas, while 3-second voice cloning and virtual-camera injection attacks defeat casual video interviews.
revenue_model: $60-120 per verified person per year, $1-3K per month platform fee, and $250 per supplier onboarding. Add a paid $2K 'ITAR access audit' as an entry product.
non_obvious_insight: In space the compliance object is not employee identity but nationality-scoped access to technical data. The unbuilt gap is attribute-based access control fed by identity proof into CAD and PLM systems. These startups fear DDTC and DoD audits and investor diligence more than hackers, so they buy compliance evidence rather than security.
first_30_days: Build a 'verified US person to Okta group' integration on an off-the-shelf IDV API. Sell a $2K ITAR access audit (export the Drive, GitHub and PLM permission lists and flag foreign-person exposures) to 5 startups via investor and accelerator introductions in Colorado Springs, Los Angeles and Huntsville. Convert audits to per-seat subscriptions before the Nov 2026 CMMC milestone.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: archTIS NC Protect, Persona (Candidate Verification), Incode Candidate Verification, Socure (workforce and candidate verification). White space: Verdict is gap, and a narrower one than the pitch implies. No product found does the specific loop the idea describes: proof of US-person status, the attribute written to an IdP through SCIM, enforcement in Drive, GitHub and PLM, and continuous drift detection. Four things fill the space today. IDV vendors (Persona, Incode, Socure, Nametag, CLEAR, Entra Verified ID) prove someone is real but do not assert or record ITAR eligibility. archTIS NC Protect enforces nationality-based access but only inside Microsoft 365 and file shares, and it trusts whatever attribute it is given. Managed-service shops (BEMO at about $4,800/month, ATX CMMC Space plus $30/user/month) deliver it as consulting with 8-month timelines. PLM vendors enforce access to an admin-typed attribute that no one has proven.

What is genuinely unserved:
- A lightweight, startup-priced system of record for US-person and permitted-data-category status, with the Empowered Official sign-off, that syncs to Okta, Entra and Google Workspace groups.
- Continuous deemed-export exposure scanning across the Drive, GitHub, Slack and PLM permission lists that startups actually use. Many are on commercial Google Workspace, which is not ITAR-compliant, and they cannot afford a GCC High or enclave migration.
- A managed workflow for licensed or TAA-scoped foreign-person exceptions, which is where hiring friction really sits.

Parts of the pitch that are not white space:
- Supplier KYB and counterfeit screening is owned by Exiger, Kharon and Sayari.
- CMMC evidence packs are owned by Secureframe, Vanta and Drata.
- Candidate and DPRK fraud detection is crowded and moving fast (Persona, Incode, Socure, Nametag, Endorsed).

Biggest structural risks:
1. The 'why now' is broken. DoD suspended CMMC Phase 2, due 10 Nov 2026, on 13 Jul 2026 and launched a 60-day reform review. Phase 1 self-assessments remain. Do not build the go-to-market around a Nov 2026 CMMC cliff.
2. Legal and product risk. The Clifford Chance settlement ($132K) shows DOJ IER penalizes employers who over-apply ITAR into citizenship discrimination. ITAR does not require hiring only US persons. Under INA 274B, employers cannot demand specific documents or run citizenship checks unevenly. A biometric 'US person' scanner sold to HR is legally delicate. Verifying green-card, asylee and refugee status by document scan is harder than a citizen passport check, and the I-9 already exists as the system of record.
3. Easy DIY. An IT admin can put an I-9-derived flag into an Okta group, so the paid value must be audit and drift detection plus the exception workflow, not the attribute itself.
4. Coverage limit. WebSearch is US-only and Crunchbase and YC searches surfaced nothing, so a stealth or very early startup on this exact wedge cannot be ruled out.

title: Insurer-Paid Total-Loss Add-On Refund Concierge
one_liner: When a financed car is totaled, the auto insurer's settlement packet is exactly what GAP and service-contract administrators demand, so the insurer pays a flat fee to have every unearned add-on refund and GAP claim filed and tracked for the claimant, who keeps 100 percent of the money.
customer: Personal-auto insurers' total-loss claims and claims-experience leaders, starting with regional and mutual carriers (roughly 50K to 1M policies; dozens to low hundreds of them, estimate) and independent-agency channels, reached through total-loss valuation and claims-platform vendors and claims TPAs as channel partners. The claimant is the beneficiary; the insurer is the payer.
problem: About one in five collision claims ends in a total loss (2M+ vehicles a year, estimate; verify with CCC-type data). Many of those cars are financed and carry rolled-in GAP, service contracts, tire-and-wheel, paint and key products that are worthless the day the car is totaled. Unearned pro-rata refunds are owed and GAP may pay a deficiency, but each has deadlines and document demands (valuation report, settlement letter, proof of loss date, payoff letter). The dealer that sold the products is long gone, the lender only sees a payoff, and the insurer never touches the retail installment contract. The claimant, already at peak frustration with the insurer, leaves money on the table, then shops for the next car and the next policy.
solution: A link in the total-loss settlement email or adjuster portal. The claimant photographs the retail installment contract (or uploads the payoff letter and dealer bill of sale). LLM extraction lists the financed add-ons and administrators; the engine computes refunds owed as of the date of loss under the contract and state rules and flags any possible GAP claim; it then auto-assembles the packet using the insurer's own valuation report, settlement letter and loss date, submits to each administrator, chases to payment, and escalates stalled cases to the state insurance department. The claimant sees a live tracker and receives 100% of recovered money (or it reduces the payoff if the loan is open, per contract). The insurer gets a dashboard of dollars recovered, days to pay and complaints avoided.
why_now: Total-loss frequency is at record levels as repair costs outpace vehicle values. Insurers just lived through 2023 to 2025 record rate increases and policyholder shopping, so retention after a claim is now a board-level metric. Claims workflows are digital end to end (e-settlement letters, text-based claims), so a link fits where a call center never did. LLMs read contract scans and administrator forms for cents, and 84-month loans with stacked add-ons mean more claimants carry unearned products than in 2019.
revenue_model: Insurer pays only for completed value: about $45 per claim where a refund or GAP payment is recovered, plus a $60K to $150K annual platform fee for integration and dashboards at a mid-size carrier (estimates to test). Channel partners take 20 to 30 percent of revenue. Illustration: a regional insurer with 8,000 total losses a year, 20% eligible with financed add-ons, is 1,600 cases at $45, about $72K a year plus platform fee. The claimant is never charged. Later modules: replacement-vehicle loan referral and title chase, and sold benchmarks of administrator refund and GAP payment speed to insurer vendor-management teams and regulators.
non_obvious_insight: The parent assumed the lender's payoff desk is the one place that sees the loan end. Total loss is a second such moment, and there the insurer, not the lender, holds the documents administrators need and has the motive to make the claimant whole. Because the insurer's paper carries a valuation report and loss date, administrators cannot stall on it the way they stall on a consumer's cancellation request. The insurer's motive is retention and complaint ratio, not the refund itself, so the fee-optics problem disappears (nobody skims the claimant's money), and the purchase comes from a claims-experience budget that already exists rather than a compliance budget that must be fought for.
first_30_days: Weeks 1 to 2: build the refund and GAP-claim rules engine for the 15 largest administrators, the claimant flow and the insurer letter template. Weeks 1 to 4: pitch 10 independent insurance agencies (who feel post-loss churn directly), 3 regional or mutual insurer claims VPs and 2 claims-technology partners. Offer a free 60-day pilot on 100 total-loss claimants with a signed LOI at $45 per recovered case if average recovery exceeds $500. Run the first 30 to 50 claimants as a concierge (analyst plus LLM), tracking opt-in rate, share with financed add-ons, average dollars and days to pay. Publish a one-page 'what a total loss leaves on the table' note from those numbers to open insurer doors.
lineage: mutation of I0109 ('Payoff-Triggered Refund Recovery for Credit Unions'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Origence (formerly CU Direct) - loan origination/indirect platform (CUDL), Assurant (F&I administrator and TPA), Unverified: consumer GAP/VSC refund-claim services (contingency), Unverified: in-house lender recovery and collections teams and BPO vendors. White space: Verification was limited. The WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted before I could run any queries, and only about 15 direct URL fetches were possible, many of which 404'd or were blocked. That leaves three points.

1. I found no direct competitor selling a payoff-triggered GAP/VSC refund plug-in to credit unions. Origence, the dominant CU indirect-lending platform, and Assurant, a major administrator, show no such product on their homepages.

2. Genuinely unserved and specific, if the market read holds:
   - A per-payoff, lender-integrated refund workflow for dealer-sold, financed add-ons at credit unions.
   - A 50-state pro-rata rules engine combined with an administrator-by-administrator cancellation-requirements database.
   - An attorney-ready audit of repossession deficiency notices that reconciles unearned add-on credits. Consumer-bankruptcy and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid are plausible buyers, because the lender's or dealer's incentive runs against the borrower.

3. Weaknesses in the idea as written, from reasoning rather than found evidence:
   - The claim that the lender never owned the product is shaky. Under many state retail installment sales acts, and under the FTC Holder Rule, the assignee or holder can carry refund and credit obligations. That helps demand, as a compliance and UDAAP driver, but it changes the pitch from 'find hidden money' to 'reduce liability'.
   - A 20-30% success fee taken from a member's own refund has poor fee optics for a credit union. It also conflicts with the idea's own member-experience rationale.
   - On payoff, the refund goes to the borrower, so the CU gets no direct economic benefit. The CU's incentive is goodwill and compliance, not revenue.
   - CU vendor due diligence and core/LOS integration will make the sales cycle slow.
   - The California SB 766 citation in the idea did not check out. The leginfo summary I fetched for the 2023-24 bill described an unrelated social-worker licensing bill. Do not rely on that cite until it is confirmed. | How this version avoids them: There is no lender integration, so Origence-style LOS vendors and credit-union procurement do not matter. Consumer refund sites depend on the borrower finding them after the fact and lack the insurer's valuation letter; here outreach lands in the settlement packet on day zero. Administrators such as Assurant are the party asked to pay, not a buyer, and the insurer's paper and regulator relationships make stalling costly. Lenders' in-house recovery teams work repossessions and charge-offs, not current-pay total losses, so there is no overlap. Claims-tech valuation and settlement vendors are channel partners because they neither read contracts nor know administrator rules; the risk is one of them building it, so lock a distribution partnership early. Unverified: I did not check for existing total-loss GAP claim-assistance vendors.

title: Remote Second-RN for Rural Night Shifts
one_liner: A pool of remote nurses that acts as the recorded, independent second person on video for narcotic waste, blood checks and high-alert drug double-checks when a rural hospital has three nurses on at 3am.
customer: Chief nursing officers and pharmacy directors at critical access hospitals (25 beds or fewer, roughly 1,300 in the US), plus the malpractice and captive insurers that cover them. Hospitals pay a monthly subscription.
problem: Policy requires a second licensed person to witness controlled-substance waste and to independently double-check insulin, heparin, blood and pediatric doses. At night at a rural hospital that second person is a nurse who is mid-code or mid-admission. Every nurse knows the witness signature is often given without actually watching. That is the most common way nurses divert drugs, and it is also how honest nurses end up with paper trails that would not survive an audit. The hospital cannot prove the witness happened. The other option is waking a colleague from another unit, which delays care.
solution: Start with a $150 tablet-and-camera cart at the dispensing cabinet. A remote RN appears on video within 60 seconds, watches the waste happen, and attests in a portal. The system keeps a time-stamped video clip and an audit log matched to the cabinet's waste records, exported as a PDF for the diversion committee. Then add two-RN blood transfusion verification, independent double-checks for high-alert drugs, and a 'second set of eyes' call for pediatric dosing. Do no EHR integration at first. Matching by timestamp is enough to sell.
why_now: The Bluesight 2026 State of Hospital Pharmacy report says about 63% of health-system leaders reported at least one diversion incident in the past year, and waste is a top diversion method because witnessing is loosely policed. Virtual nursing has become normal since 2024, and the Nurse Licensure Compact now covers most states, so one remote nurse can cover many hospitals. State Rural Health Transformation Program money is flowing, with every state having posted at least one funding opportunity by August 2026, and workforce and quality dollars can pay for this. Whether remote-video witnessing is acceptable is mostly a hospital-policy and pharmacy and therapeutics committee decision, but each state's board of pharmacy and nursing board should be checked before launch.
revenue_model: $1,500-2,500 per hospital per month, plus a per-event fee for transfusion and double-check calls above a set volume. A typical rural ED has 10-25 waste events a night at 2-3 minutes each, so one remote RN can cover roughly 8-12 hospitals per night. Estimated gross margin is 40-50%. A secondary revenue line is a discount arrangement with medical liability insurers, who benefit from the audit trail.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone selling diversion software (analytics, cabinet data mining, waste-testing) tries to detect diversion after the fact. Insiders know the root problem is that no real second person exists at night in a small hospital. You do not need better detection. You need to supply the missing colleague, cheaply and on camera. The service also protects honest nurses, who will therefore support it and not resist it.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 per-diem or retired RNs with compact licenses who want remote night hours at $35-40/hr. Use an off-the-shelf tablet with a recording app and a simple web portal that produces the PDF log. Offer free 30-day pilots to two critical access hospitals through the founder nurse's own pharmacy director and CNO. Get the pilot approved as a policy amendment at the pharmacy and therapeutics committee. Convert to a $1,500 monthly contract after 30 days if the audit log is shown to the diversion committee and the hospital's insurer.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: MIDAS Healthcare Solutions (MidasVIEW / Anytime Witness, aka V.I.E.W.), BD Pyxis Med Link Queue & Waste, Avel eCare, VirtuAlly (with Teledigm Health). White space: Nobody I found sells a shared, pooled, live remote-RN witness subscription to critical access hospitals. The specific gaps are:
(1) Live human supply. MidasVIEW replaces the second person with recorded video reviewed later. Pyxis remote witness still needs a colleague on shift. Virtual-nursing vendors cover admissions, discharges, sitters and documentation. Remote pharmacy vendors cover order verification. Nobody provides a licensed second person on demand at 3am.
(2) Transfusion, high-alert and pediatric double-checks. Asynchronous video cannot substitute for a live independent check before administration. Remote IDC is documented as feasible but under-evidenced, and only a few institutions do it (ONS 2024).
(3) Small-hospital fit. MidasVIEW pilots are at tertiary and children's hospitals. Small facilities lag on diversion controls: only 57% of single facilities actively monitor camera footage, and CAHs lack pharmacy staff to review video the next day.
(4) Insurer-linked audit trail. No diversion vendor sells to liability or captive insurers.
The wedge is narrow and time-limited. Avel eCare, VirtuAlly and the telepharmacy vendors could add a witness line quickly, and MidasVIEW could add live witness routing.

title: Courtroom ETA: Call-Time Network for Family Court
one_liner: A 'FlightAware for family court calendars' that texts litigants, lawyers and freelance reporters and interpreters their predicted call time, giving the queue away and selling the same feed to the professionals who lose half-day minimums waiting.
customer: Start: DV survivors and family litigants (free, via legal-aid and DV org sponsors) and solo family-law attorneys ($29/month). Paying side by month 6: freelance court reporters, interpreters and appearance attorneys who buy call-time alerts to hop between hearings. Later: courts, which pay for staggered 'time-certain' calendars.
problem: Family calendars run on the 8:30 cattle call: 30-40 matters set at one time and called in an order nobody can see. Parties, including survivors who may wait near their abuser, sit in a hallway for hours. Attorneys burn billable time (a solo lawyer's 2-hour wait costs $400-600, an assumption to verify). Reporters, interpreters and appearance counsel price by the half day because no one can predict a 15-minute call time. The parent's dispatch model needed that prediction but assumed it was a feature, when it is the missing infrastructure for every short-hearing service.
solution: Inverted product: prediction first, services second. Month 1-6 product: an SMS bot for two departments in one courthouse. A litigant or attorney texts a case number and gets 'about 45 minutes; you are 9th of 34'. Data comes from the public daily calendar, historical durations by hearing type and judge, and check-ins: people text 'called' or 'out' from the hallway (not from inside the courtroom, where phones may be restricted), plus paid spotters logging call order at $18/hour for the first 20 court days. Publish a per-department 'wait report card' as press and leverage. The same feed then powers a services layer, with reporters, interpreters and appearance attorneys buying alerts and booking one hearing at a time, which turns the parent's marketplace into the second product. Endgame: the call-time index becomes the standard that courts license to stagger calendars.
why_now: After the FVAP decision the gap in recorded hearings is public news. Courts, legal aid and press now treat family-court process failures as a story. Cheap SMS, LLM-based calendar parsing and speech-to-text make the data layer nearly free, while calendar data has been public but unused for years. The reporter shortage forces reporters to hop to survive, and the shortage gives them an incentive to pay for the ETA.
revenue_model: Free for litigants (sponsored by DV legal aid, foundation and IOLTA-type grants). $29/month for attorneys. $99-299/month per reporter, interpreter or appearance attorney for alerts and hop scheduling, plus a booking fee (10-15%) once the per-hearing marketplace exists. Courts pay for calendar analytics and a staggering tool ($20-60K per court per year, an assumption) after the wait report cards create pressure. Bottom-up illustration to test: 40 family departments x 30 matters x 2 parties is about 2,400 party-attendances/day in one large county.
non_obvious_insight: The reporting shortage is a symptom of an information problem: half-day minimums exist because the call time is unknowable. Give the information away to the crowd and charge the people who can turn it into utilization. Each check-in improves the ETA for everyone else in the department (network effect), so density in a courthouse is the moat, and the data is a cornered resource no reporter agency can copy without the crowd. It also fixes the parent's legal flaw: it needs no remote reporting, only public calendars and voluntary check-ins.
first_30_days: Week 1: choose the two busiest family departments in one large county, hire two spotters (retired court watchers or paralegal students) and log call order and durations for 20 court days. Week 2: build a Twilio SMS bot with a manual ETA rule (calendar position x median duration by hearing type). Week 3: recruit 10 solo attorneys and 2 DV legal-aid groups as first users, and 3 freelance interpreters or reporters as paying alerts customers. Week 4: publish the first department wait report card and test whether hallway wait shrinks and whether any reporter will pay $99/month. Day 180 target: 300 active attorneys and litigants in one courthouse, 20 paying professionals, and a second courthouse.
lineage: mutation of I0248 ('Fifteen-Minute Court Reporting for Family Law Hearings'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Steno (Steno Agency Inc.), DirectDep, StenoScout, Incumbent agencies (Veritext, Esquire, Combs Reporting, Coalition Court Reporters). White space: Nobody offers flat-fee coverage of 15-minute California family-law hearings. That is because the core mechanic, private reporters dialing in from anywhere, is currently barred. Gov. Code 69959 says 'Remote court reporting shall not be used by courts to make the record of any court proceedings' and defines it as a stenographer not present in the courtroom (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959/). The only exception, Gov. Code 69959.5, allows remote reporting only by 'full-time official reporters ... employed by the participating superior court', physically in a court facility, in 13 pilot counties, capped at 10-20% of reporters (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959-5/). San Diego's court page states 'the court is prohibited by law from allowing remote court reporting for any court proceeding' (https://sdcourt.ca.gov/sdcourt/generalinformation/resourcelists/courtreporterinformation). The idea's claim that AB 3013 'opened remote reporting' to a private platform is wrong. Unserved and still legal: (1) physical-presence short-hearing coverage, where one pro tem covers several departments in the same courthouse using calendar-based duration prediction, and no vendor markets a per-hearing SKU; (2) a scheduling and utilization layer sold to courts to fill pro tem and official reporter slots, aimed at hiring and retention (the ruling names 'pro tem reporters paid by the court' as a compliance route, and court reporter counsel is calling on courts to lift hiring freezes); (3) fast certified transcripts of court electronic recordings for attorneys who need appellate-grade records. The white space is real but is a legal-regime bet on remote reporting being opened to private reporters, plus a narrow physical-hopping wedge. It is not a software-only wedge. Court reporter unions opposed AB 3013 and are a political headwind. | How this version avoids them: None of the parent's competitors predicts call time. Steno, DirectDep and StenoScout are booking marketplaces for depositions and would be buyers of the feed, not rivals. Incumbent agencies sell half-day pro tem, which is what the ETA erodes. eScribers and Verbit handle records after the fact, and the AB 3013 pilot is court-employed reporting. The one adjacent category I could not check (search budget exhausted) is court-date reminder apps, which remind people of the date but, as far as I know, do not rank queue position within a calendar. Verify that before building. Main risks: courts restricting phone use or check-ins, and calendar data quality, so the first release relies on spotters and public calendars.

title: Work-Permit Gap Desk for Frontline Employers
one_liner: Employer-paid, pre-cliff delay suits for workers whose EAD renewals are pending, sold to home-care, nursing and staffing employers as a per-worker maintenance plan instead of a one-off legal purchase.
customer: HR and compliance directors or owners of 150-1,500 employee home-care agencies, skilled-nursing operators and staffing firms in the NYC-metro and New Jersey area (workers resident in E.D.N.Y., S.D.N.Y. and D.N.J., where delay suits most often end in agency action), each with hundreds of workers on time-limited work authorization (asylum-pending, adjustment-pending, parole and DACA categories). The worker is the lawyer's client; the employer is the payer and the buyer of the platform. Later channel: I-9/E-Verify vendors, PEOs and state home-care and staffing associations.
problem: Employers eat the cliff. Since the 540-day automatic EAD extension ended for renewals filed from late Oct 2025, a worker whose I-765 renewal is still pending on the expiry date must come off the schedule. A care agency watches a predictable slice of its workforce disappear for months, pays replacement and onboarding costs, and has no lever to pull. Its HR team already tracks every expiry date for I-9 compliance, but that process ends at 'alert' with no remedy step. Immigration counsel are hired by individuals or for petitions like H-1B and PERM, never as an operations service for frontline workforces, so this problem has no owner.
solution: Gap Desk in three parts. (1) Free EAD Gap Calculator: HR uploads employee ID, EAD category code and expiry date (no names), and gets the projected number of workers who will hit expiry before a decision, priced in lost margin and replacement cost. (2) Enrolled program: the employer offers a voluntary benefit to every employee with time-limited work authorization regardless of nationality (to limit anti-discrimination exposure). The platform watches filing date against expiry; when a ledger-set trigger fires (case beyond posted time and expiry approaching), it obtains the worker's consent and files through a panel of federal-admitted attorneys at a flat fee. Structure: the worker is the client, the employer pays as a third-party payer with informed consent (independent judgment and confidentiality preserved), and the employer sees only a status date. (3) Bridge kit: job-hold and leave templates and a reinstatement re-verification checklist so the employer keeps the seat during the gap. Out of scope by design: TPS terminations, revoked parole and denials, which are not delay problems.
why_now: The auto-extension ended in Oct 2025, and Mandamus.com's case-law tracker calls I-765 mandamus a 'primary remedy' since then, so the cliff is new and the remedy is proven. Expiry dates are known 6-12 months ahead, so the risk is forecastable. Care-sector labor is scarce, making each lost seat expensive. LLM drafting plus a per-district ledger lets a panel attorney turn a routine I-765 suit in about an hour, making a $1,750 flat fee profitable. The USAO's 45-90 day resolution pattern matches the length of a typical gap.
revenue_model: Employer pays $5 per covered worker per month (monitoring, calculator, case management) plus $2,000 per triggered case: $1,750 paid directly to the panel attorney and $250 to the platform as a flat administrative fee. Never a percentage of the legal fee. Illustration for a 400-worker agency: $24k/year subscription plus about 20 triggered cases (about $5k platform, $35k to attorneys). Assumption to validate in pilots: a 90-day gap costs an agency roughly $5-10k in lost margin and replacement, so 20 avoided gaps clearly exceed the roughly $59k program cost. Year 2: I-9 vendors and PEOs resell for a cut of the subscription only.
non_obvious_insight: The party with the most to lose from a stuck case is the employer, yet employers have never been the buyer because immigration law treats the individual as the client; third-party payer rules allow the employer to pay while the worker stays the client. Once the employer pays, the product changes character: expiry dates are known a year ahead, so demand is a forecastable renewal calendar and recurring subscription instead of lumpy, panicked legal purchases. And the employer's I-9 tickler is already the distribution asset, since it holds exactly the dates that trigger the suit.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: build the calculator as a spreadsheet plus web form and run it on anonymized expiry lists from 3 friendly employers. Days 1-10: sign 2-3 panel attorneys admitted in E.D.N.Y., S.D.N.Y. and D.N.J. at $1,750 flat and get an employment-law read on third-party-payer, anti-discrimination and prepaid-legal-plan rules. Days 7-30: contact about 60 NYC-metro and NJ home-care agencies and staffing firms through state association events and LinkedIn, lead with their own calculator output, and close 3 paid pilots at about $2,500/month concierge plus per-case fees. Go/no-go: at least one employer with a real expiring cohort authorizes a filing within 30 days, and outcomes are logged to seed the ledger.
lineage: mutation of I1062 ('Delay-Suit Rails for Stuck Immigration Cases'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Bertollini / Mandamus.com (immigration mandamus boutique), Docketwise (immigration case-management software), Alma (tryalma.com, immigration law firm plus tech), Boundless (consumer immigration services). White space: Important caveat first. The WebSearch budget was already spent (200 of 200) before I started, so I ran no web searches at all. I used direct fetches of guessed or known URLs, CourtListener's API and GitHub search. This means 'no direct software competitor found' is weaker evidence than normal. One attempt to load a Google results page returned nothing and was not used. Before committing, someone should run 6-8 real searches (for example 'mandamus AI immigration', 'delay lawsuit software immigration attorneys', Crunchbase, YC, and the AILA and AIC toolkits).

What I found: no software or platform that sells attorney-signed, white-label mandamus filing plus a per-district rules library plus outcome analytics to solo immigration lawyers. The only direct-service players are boutique law firms selling the suit to end clients. Mandamus.com does this at $5,000 plus $500 and gives away templates, and the practice-management incumbent Docketwise has no such feature. The open data (CourtListener) and free guides make the raw ingredients cheap for anyone.

The genuinely unserved wedge is narrow. It is a pre-filing 'will this get mooted or dismissed here' triage, based on real district-by-form-type outcome data, plus a ready-to-file pack for routine delays in the districts where the government usually adjudicates rather than litigates (per Mandamus.com's own data: EDNY, D. Conn., DNJ and EDMI at 83-85% voluntary dismissal after agency action).

Parts of the pitch look weak against what I found:
(1) Nationality-hold suits look poor. Per Mandamus.com's summary of 13 D.D.C. delay decisions from June to August 2026, the government won all 13. Judge Leon in the consolidated Ivanov case found the categorical pause unexplained but dismissed the delay and mandamus counts under TRAC and limited relief to named plaintiffs. A 'nationality hold' template is a liability, not a hook.
(2) S.D. Tex., one of the five launch districts, is hostile. Cheejati v. Blinken (5th Cir. 2024) bars I-485 delay claims on jurisdictional grounds, and DOJ there files motions to dismiss rather than negotiate.
(3) Buckhannon: when USCIS simply adjudicates, the plaintiff is not a prevailing party and can't recover EAJA fees (typically $4,000-$12,000 only if a consent order is obtained). The flat fee holds up, but the 'forced deadline' product should be structured around consent orders.
(4) The '6-10 hour learning curve' is being eroded by free content and general AI drafting.
(5) The data moat is thin. CourtListener docket data is free, and the boutique firms already publish their own district stats. | How this version avoids them: Mandamus.com sells single suits to individuals at $5,000 with SEO funnels and cannot run a workforce calendar for an employer. I-9/E-Verify vendors track expiry dates but stop at an alert (not verified in this research); they are channel partners, not rivals. Docketwise and Boundless serve firms and individuals on petitions, not employer-paid remedies. Alma sells O-1/EB-1 strategy to companies for high-skill hires, not frontline EAD renewals. Large corporate immigration firms serve professionals where ticket sizes are big; a $1,750 frontline case is below their radar (unverified). DoNotPay and free pro se guides cannot give an employer a managed, attorney-signed service with status reporting. Employer ownership of the buyer relationship is the wedge none of them hold.

title: AltSchool Without Buildings: Disability Programs in Host Schools
one_liner: AltSchool burned $170M+ building its own schools; in Texas, the new voucher money can only reach accredited schools with two years of history, so rent that eligibility by running clinician-led disability programs inside half-empty accredited private schools.
customer: Payer: Texas families with children on IEPs holding Texas Education Freedom Accounts (about $10k standard, up to $30k for IEP students at accredited private schools). Partner: small accredited private schools, often church schools, with empty classrooms. Supply: speech-language pathologists, BCBAs and dyslexia therapists who want to run a program.
problem: TEFA rules require private schools to be accredited and to have operated two consecutive school years, and microschool or learning-pod students get only $2,000. Families holding $30k accounts cannot find seats with real special-ed capacity. Eligible incumbents have buildings but no special-ed expertise. Clinicians have expertise but no eligibility.
solution: An operating company signs a host agreement with an accredited school. The school enrolls the students as school of record and receives the TEFA funds. We supply a clinical director, staff, structured-literacy or ABA-informed curriculum, IEP compliance, the annual norm-referenced testing TEFA requires for grades 3-12, and ESA billing reconciliation. Start with 8-10 student cohorts (dyslexia and autism support). Confirm with each host's accreditor that a program-within-a-school structure is acceptable.
why_now: TEFA's first year is starting (2026-27): $1B in funding, more than 130,000 applications in the first three weeks, roughly 100,000 families expected. Texas public schools lost about 76,000 students this year and are closing dozens of campuses. Federal special-ed enforcement was hollowed out (OSEP layoffs in October 2025, with the office reportedly moving to HHS in June 2026), so parents are looking for alternatives.
revenue_model: Management fee of about 20-25% of ESA revenue per student ($6-7.5k per $30k student, so $60-75k per 10-student program per year), with a 15-20% host share; one-time program-design fee ($3-5k) per host; compliance and reconciliation SaaS later.
non_obvious_insight: AltSchool's mistake was building schools. In Texas the moat is accreditation plus a two-year operating history, which are other people's assets, so partner instead of build. Empty church-school classrooms, underemployed clinicians and $30k accounts form a three-way arbitrage that only exists because of the new rules.
first_30_days: List about 150 small accredited private schools in DFW, Houston, San Antonio and Austin using accreditor directories. Send heads of school a one-page economics sheet. Recruit 10 clinicians via LinkedIn and SLP/BCBA Facebook groups. Sign 1-2 pilot hosts for a January 2027 cohort and collect pre-enrollment interest from TEFA parent groups. First revenue is host design fees, with per-student revenue starting once enrollments transfer.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Fusion Academy (Nord Anglia), Brightmont Academy, Prenda (microschool platform), KaiPod Learning. White space: Research caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before any searches ran, so this verdict rests on about 30 direct page fetches, not the planned 6-12 searches. Google-style discovery of funded startups was not possible, and the negative finding below is unproven. Crunchbase (403), the Comptroller TEFA program pages (404), TEPSAC (503) and several news sites failed.

What the fetches found: no direct competitor was located that runs clinician-led disability programs inside host accredited private schools as the school-of-record structure and bills against TEFA. Adjacent players cover each piece separately.
- Learning-differences schools that build their own campuses: Fusion, Brightmont, Rawson Saunders, Fairhill.
- Microschool platforms: Prenda, KaiPod, Primer.
- Clinician marketplaces: Presence.
- Outside operators embedded in private schools: Catapult.

The unserved wedge is the three-way structure itself. It is a management company that supplies the clinical director, staff, IEP compliance, norm-referenced testing and ESA reconciliation inside a host school. It targets IEP families holding up to $30k accounts in metro Texas in the first TEFA year.

Three risks decide whether the white space is real, and none is resolved:
1. **Legality and accreditor acceptance.** Statute text says a private school must be accredited by a TEPSAC-recognized organization and have continuously operated a campus for at least two school years. It does not address programs within a school or microschools. If the Comptroller, TEA or the accreditor treats a hosted program as a separate campus, or as renting accreditation, the model fails. A 100% pass-through of the ESA to the host with a 20-25% management fee could also draw scrutiny.
2. **Incumbents and hosts.** Existing specialist schools already have eligibility and expertise and may simply expand. Host schools take on IEP compliance liability and reputational risk.
3. **Unit economics.** A 10-student cohort at 20-25% yields $60-75k a year, before clinician cost. Whether that covers a BCBA or dyslexia therapist plus a clinical director was not tested.

title: Dispatch-Eligibility Registry for Backup Generators
one_liner: Become the neutral system of record for whether each backup generator may legally run for the grid right now, starting as a Texas SB 6 compliance product and growing into the rail that ERCOT, PJM, utilities and aggregators check before dispatch.
customer: First buyer: environmental and compliance leads at 75 MW+ data centers in Texas, who face the SB 6 disclosure and deploy-on-direction duty and must not violate emissions limits. Then PJM colos that must prove permit compliance to state air agencies and counties. Then DR aggregators, utilities and RTOs that consume the dispatch-eligibility certificate through an API. Later expansion is to hospitals, water utilities and telecom, where the wider standby generator fleet is far larger (widely cited estimates run into the hundreds of GW, which I have not verified).
problem: Backup generation is the largest idle block of capacity, but it can only be called if three things are true at the moment of the call: the engine is permitted for that use, it has hours left in the rolling year, and the trigger is a legally recognized emergency. Today the answer sits in permit PDFs, OEM dashboards and spreadsheets. Regulators cannot see it, so they say no. Aggregators carry enforcement risk and cannot prove compliance. Communities suspect the worst about diesel, which sinks permits. Nobody can be sure that dispatching an engine on a given day will not breach a cap.
solution: A run-hour ledger and certificate service. Step one is software only: an ingest of permit conditions (LLM-structured, attorney-reviewed) plus monthly or continuous hour-meter data from BMS exports, OEM telemetry or a read-only J1939/Modbus tap, with non-resettable meter attestation as a fallback. It computes remaining permitted hours per engine, tags every run with its legal basis (test, maintenance, emergency, directed deployment), auto-generates regulator deviation and compliance reports, and publishes a public disclosure page. Step two is a machine-readable Dispatch Eligibility Certificate (open schema, mapped to OpenADR 3.0 and IEEE 2030.5 event payloads, which carry price and event signals but not legal eligibility). RTOs, utilities and aggregators query it before calling an engine. Step three, once regulators accept the format, is clearing and settlement of permit-cleared MW across the registry.
why_now: Texas SB 6 (2025) makes disclosure and directed deployment of backup generation a legal duty for 75 MW+ loads, with an explicit emissions carve-out, so demand for exactly this record is forced by regulation. PJM is filing a reliability backstop and connect-and-manage framework, and Pennsylvania is pushing bring-your-own-generation rules. Turbines are sold out to about 2029-30. LLM extraction of permit conditions cuts the cost of structuring each site from consultant weeks to hours plus attorney QA. None of this existed at scale in 2019.
revenue_model: Onboarding and permit structuring of $15-40k per facility. SaaS of $3-6k per engine per year, which is about $25-50k a year for a 20 MW fleet of 8-10 engines. Aggregators and utilities pay a verification fee of roughly 0.5-1% of dispatch revenue that runs through certificates, and lenders, insurers and RTOs license the data ($100-300k a year). Illustrative scale: 5,000 engines is about $20M ARR, and the roughly 22,000 data center engines implied by 55 GW at 2.5 MW each is about $90M. Wider standby fleets would multiply that several times.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce commodity is not megawatts or even permits. It is remaining permitted run-hours, a finite annual budget per engine, and nobody keeps that ledger neutrally. Whoever holds the ledger regulators trust becomes the rail everyone else must query, and the aggregators cannot build it because they profit from dispatch and cannot credibly police themselves. This inverts the parent: instead of pushing MW into the grid and hoping regulators follow, make regulators' comfort the product. Regulators have said no partly because they cannot see run hours. The registry supplies that visibility and could become the reason a permit is granted with conditions. It also creates network economies (every consumer of the certificate raises the value of being in it) and switching costs, since compliance history is an audit record.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: ship a software-only SB 6 and Title V ledger MVP (permit parsing plus hour-meter ingest plus report generation) and publish the Dispatch Eligibility Certificate v0.1 schema openly. Days 5-30: contact compliance leads at 20 Texas 75 MW+ operators and offer five pilots at $15k with a fixed-format SB 6 backup-generation disclosure pack. Days 10-30: hold informal briefings with TCEQ and VA DEQ staff to test whether an electronic ledger is acceptable as a compliance record, and get consumption LOIs (free API in exchange for feedback) from at least one aggregator. The riskiest assumption is regulator acceptance, so test it in the first month. Retain an air attorney to review the legal-basis tagging.
lineage: mutation of I0836 ('Air-Permit Unlock for Idle Data Center Diesel'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Voltus, CPower, Enchanted Rock (ERock), Trinity Consultants (data center and power team). White space: Verification caveat: the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted, so no search-engine, Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or TechCrunch queries could be run. I did about 30 direct page fetches and 2 GitHub searches instead. The GitHub searches found no open-source tool for this. I found no company selling a fixed-price 'permit-to-dispatch' package for existing data center diesel fleets (permit modification, emissions retrofit financing, telemetry, PJM enrollment and M&V). That is absence of evidence from a constrained search, not proof that none exists.

What appears unserved:
(1) A productized, per-state permit playbook tied to capacity outcomes. Trinity-type consultants sell hourly, per-project permitting. DR aggregators (Voltus, CPower) sell enrollment and revenue share. Generator OEMs and ERock sell hardware. Nobody I found owns the seam between them.
(2) Retrofit financing on the subset of engines that need it.
(3) A permit-headroom dataset across Title V and minor-source files.

The binding constraint is legal, not competitive. Under 40 CFR 63.6640(f), as summarized from Cornell LII, emergency engines are limited to 100 hours a year for maintenance, testing and emergencies, with at most 50 of those for non-emergency use. The 50 hours cannot be used for peak shaving or non-emergency demand response, and cannot generate income or serve a financial arrangement with another entity. Only narrow exceptions exist, dispatched by local authorities for transmission and distribution limits. Selling emergency-designated diesel as PJM capacity therefore likely requires reclassifying engines as non-emergency, which triggers stricter engine standards (Tier 4 or SCR-type controls), plus state NOx limits and possible major-source permitting. That is why the founder's 'retrofit the subset' step is likely the real cost and risk. It is also why incumbents have stayed away. The wedge exists only where the permit and retrofit math actually closes.

Other risks: PJM DR accreditation rules and limited-duration derating, which I could not verify because the PJM manual fetch returned only a table of contents. Local opposition to diesel. Hyperscalers and utilities choosing gas or battery capacity instead. | How this version avoids them: Voltus and CPower are dispatchers, and Voltus's Google deal covers batteries and thermostats, not generators or permits. They are conflicted as ledger-keepers and are natural certificate consumers, so we court them as design partners. ERock sells and operates its own gas hardware. OEM telemetry (Cat, Cummins and similar) is per-brand, not independent, and does not map runs to permit legal basis. DCIM and EHS software log air data but do not answer 'may I dispatch this engine now'. OpenADR and IEEE 2030.5 carry signals, not legality, so we build on them rather than compete. Trinity sells hourly permit projects, not a live neutral record, and could be a channel for onboarding. Note that the comparisons to OEM, DCIM and EHS vendors rest on my background knowledge, not verified this session.

title: Phantom Pipeline Audits for Utility Rate-Case Intervenors
one_liner: Sell to the ratepayers who pay for phantom load, meaning industrial customer groups and state consumer advocates in IRP, CPCN and large-load-tariff dockets, a testimony-ready audit of how much of a utility's confidential data-center pipeline is physically real.
customer: Buyer: counsel and expert budgets of (a) industrial customer intervenor groups (steel, paper, chemicals) that fear being left with stranded data-center infrastructure costs, and (b) state consumer advocate offices, in dockets where the utility's generation or transmission request rests on a data-center pipeline. Later: county and city governments facing abatement votes ($15-30K packs), and utility credit and equity analysts who subscribe to a Phantom Ratio Index. The sales path is through the law firms and staff attorneys who run these dockets.
problem: Utilities are asking commissions to approve gigawatts of gas plants and transmission justified by 'signed' large-load pipelines. The pipeline exhibits are confidential or anonymized ('Customer A, 400 MW'). Intervenor experts can only critique them top-down with econometrics, because nobody checks entries one by one against the physical trail. The evidence that pipelines are inflated is broad: an EPRI survey found none of 10 utilities with requests of 50%+ of peak expected actual 5-year load above 35% of peak, and Exelon's estimates fell about 40% after stricter collateral. But the intervenor cannot show which megawatts are fake, and a project shopped to two utilities is counted twice.
solution: A 'realization audit' delivered through counsel. Under the docket's protective order, the desk takes the utility's pipeline exhibit (MW, county or substation, in-service date, status). It scores each entry against the public trail: air permits and generator counts, deed or option and rezoning agenda items, water and stormwater filings, principal and LLC cross-matching across states, and whether the claimed in-service date is feasible given published equipment lead times. The output is a probability-weighted realized MW by year with confidence bands, a list of duplicate-counted megawatts across utilities, and a testimony-ready exhibit sponsored by a credentialed expert witness (a retired utility planner or former commission staffer on retainer). Where entries are fully anonymized, the audit triangulates from county-level permit and land-use activity and asks the commission to compel the identities under protective order. The same work product seeds a quarterly Phantom Ratio Index by utility and state.
why_now: Electricity affordability is a live political issue in the November 2026 midterms, and data-center load forecasts are the key contested input in a wave of 2026 large-load tariff, IRP and generation-certificate dockets. Regulators are already moving on transparency (Texas ownership audit, Pennsylvania's Aug 18 executive order for projects over 25 MW), so intervenors now have standing to ask for pipeline detail. Cleanview-style permit trackers plus OCR'd county records have made the public-trail checks cheap enough to run per docket at a fixed fee.
revenue_model: $40-120K fixed fee per docket engagement, covering the audit, exhibit and expert sponsorship, paid from intervenor budgets and industrial group dues. $15-30K county and municipal packs. A $25-60K/yr Phantom Ratio Index seat for credit analysts, muni and equity desks and hedge funds. Year-1 target: 6-10 dockets ($600K-$900K) plus early index subscribers, with about 60% gross margin because the expert and analyst time is billable.
non_obvious_insight: The parties who lose most from phantom load are not the utility's five planners but the other ratepayers, and they already have lawyers, a procedural calendar and an expert budget. The docket schedule sets the deadline, so no procurement cycle is needed. The natural competitors, utility-aligned engineering consultancies, are conflicted when the audit target is their client's pipeline, which makes an adversarial audit counter-positioned rather than just different. And duplicate-counting is only visible from outside: each utility sees only its own queue, but an auditor working in four states sees the same project in three pipelines. The adversarial work therefore seeds the national duplicate registry from a side no utility-aligned vendor can reach.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: list every live docket in 6-8 states where a large-load pipeline is in dispute, using public commission dockets, and note testimony deadlines in the next 60-120 days plus who the intervenors and their counsel are. Days 10-20: build a free 2-page 'public trail check' of one utility's publicly disclosed data-center announcements, using licensed permit data plus deeds and permits, and send it to 15 intervenor counsel and consumer advocate staff. Recruit a credentialed expert witness (retired planner or ex-commission staff). Days 20-30: close 1-2 paid engagements at about $40K, one with an industrial group and one with a consumer advocate. Kill test: if counsel will not pay $40K for a per-entry audit because their econometric expert already covers it, the intervenor thesis is dead and the index is the fallback.
lineage: mutation of I0079 ('Phantom Load Vetting Desk for Rural Utilities'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: GridUnity, Clean Power Research (PowerClerk), Enverus, LandGate. White space: I found no direct competitor. No startup, consultancy or association was selling a utility-side, per-inquiry 'is this developer physically real' memo with a recommended collateral amount and milestone-gated study structure. The gap is real but narrow.

What is unserved: (1) External physical-trail verification for small utilities, meaning air-permit generator counts vs claimed MW, recorded deeds and options, LLC principal cross-checks, and OEM or EPC evidence. GridUnity and PowerClerk track applicant-supplied data but do not verify it. Enverus, LandGate and GridCARE serve the developer side. (2) A cross-utility duplicate-request registry. Texas SB 6 mandates duplicate-request disclosure only inside ERCOT. Outside ERCOT there is no pooled registry. Developers do file the same project with several utilities (Latitude Media, Utility Dive). (3) Packaging for 5-person co-op engineering staffs: I found no NRECA vetting checklist or tool, and no small-utility-specific vendor.

Serious weaknesses the founder must address:
- Regulation and tariffs are substituting for vetting. Collateral, study fees and site-control mandates make the applicant self-prove. Exelon cut its estimates about 40% after stricter collateral. AEP Ohio's pipeline fell by more than half after study fees of up to $100K (https://techstartups.com/2026/09/01/ai-data-centers-request-700-gw-of-u-s-power-but-much-of-the-demand-may-be-an-illusion/). Once a co-op requires a deposit, site control and a signed LOI, much of the 12-point test becomes documents the applicant hands over.
- Texas SB 6 / 16 TAC 25.194 applies only in ERCOT (https://www.dlapiper.com/en-us/insights/publications/2026/03/texas-proposes-new-interconnection-standards-for-large-electric-loads). The 'small utilities in neighboring states get the displaced phantoms' claim is plausible but I found no evidence for it.
- Several tests may not be observable by an outsider. OEM order acknowledgments and financing letters are confidential, and real developers often approach the utility before ordering equipment.
- Regulators are absorbing the LLC-transparency piece. Texas ordered an audit requiring true-ownership disclosure, and Pennsylvania issued an August 18 executive order for projects over 25 MW.
- Big engineering consultancies could add this as a service line. I could not verify whether they already do. My web-search budget ran out before I could check. | How this version avoids them: GridUnity, PowerClerk, Camus and Ascend sell software to utilities as vendors, run on applicant-supplied data and cannot be adversarial. Enverus (load forecasting for utilities), LandGate and GridCARE serve utilities or developers. Cleanview is a free tracker with no per-entry audit, expert witness or confidential pipeline access, so it is a data input, not a rival. ZEG advises developers and utilities. NRECA serves co-ops and has nothing for IOU dockets. Utility-aligned consultancies (Burns & McDonnell and similar) are conflicted by their clients, and existing intervenor-side experts do top-down forecast critique, not entry-level physical-trail verification. The buyer, the payer and the deliverable are all different from the parent's co-op memo, so nobody in the parent's research is selling to the same person.
